text: Abraham of Nathpar was an East Syriac monastic writer active in the first half of the seventh century, during a period of strong growth in the monastic movement of the Church of the East. Few details of his life are securely known. He wrote short ascetic treatises on the spiritual life, including a work on the solitaries, which deals with the discipline and inner life of monks living in seclusion. His writings belong to the wider tradition of Syriac ascetical literature.

Abū al-Majdalus, also called al-Majdalus, was a Christian writer in Arabic. He is known only as the author of a commentary on the Nicene Creed, the Tafsīr al-amāna, which explains the creed of the councils of Nicaea and Constantinople. Little is known about his life. His date and church affiliation are uncertain. He has been placed in the tenth century and was probably a Melkite, but neither point is firmly established.

Acacius of Beroea (c. 322–437) was a Syrian monk from near Antioch who opposed Arianism and became bishop of Beroea (Aleppo) in 378. As a priest he and Paul wrote to Epiphanius of Salamis, and their letter led to the Panarion. He went to Rome against Apollinaris and attended the Council of Constantinople in 381. Later he joined the opposition to John Chrysostom at the Synod of the Oak in 403. In the Nestorian controversy he worked to reconcile Cyril of Alexandria with the Eastern bishops. A few of his Greek letters survive.

Acacius of Melitene (died after 437, perhaps c. 438) was metropolitan bishop of Melitene in the Roman province of Armenia Secunda, in eastern Anatolia. He strongly opposed Nestorius and was a close ally of Cyril of Alexandria at the Council of Ephesus in 431, where he delivered a homily. He wrote two letters to Cyril and received two from him in return. He also warned against the teaching of Theodore of Mopsuestia. Only a few homilies and letters connected with the Nestorian controversy survive.

Adomnán of Iona (also Adamnan or Eunan; born in the 620s, died 704) was an Irish monk who served as the ninth abbot of Iona from 679 until his death. He was also a statesman and canon lawyer, and he is venerated as a saint. His Life of Columba, probably written between 697 and 700, is the most important surviving work from early medieval Scotland. He also wrote De Locis Sanctis, a description of the holy places of the Christian East that drew largely on the account of the Frankish bishop Arculf. In 697, at the Synod of Birr, he promulgated the Law of Innocents (Cáin Adomnáin), which protected women, children and other non-combatants.

Adso of Montier-en-Der (Adso Dervensis, c. 910/920–992) was a Benedictine abbot of Montier-en-Der in France who died on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Most of what is known of his life comes from a single source of questioned reliability. Tradition presents him as a monastic reformer, a scholar and the author of five saints' lives. His best-known work is a letter on the Antichrist, De ortu et tempore Antichristi, addressed to Queen Gerberga. It draws on biblical exegesis and Sibylline lore but is written in the style of a saint's life. It was copied many times and shaped later medieval apocalyptic thought.

Ælfric of Eynsham (c. 955 – c. 1010) was an English Benedictine monk and abbot. He was a pupil of Æthelwold of Winchester and a leading figure of the Benedictine reform. He taught at Cerne Abbas and became the first abbot of Eynsham around 1005. He was a prolific writer of Old English prose. His works include two series of Catholic Homilies (c. 989–995), the Lives of Saints, biblical translations and paraphrases, and pastoral letters. He also wrote a Latin Grammar in English, a Glossary and a Colloquy for teaching Latin. These earned him the name Ælfric Grammaticus.

Aeneas of Gaza (died c. 518) was a Greek rhetorician and Christian philosopher of Neoplatonic background. He belonged to the rhetorical school of Gaza in Byzantine Palestine, which flourished in the fifth and sixth centuries. With Procopius of Gaza and Zacharias Scholasticus, he is sometimes grouped as the "Gaza Triad". His best-known work is the Theophrastus, a dialogue on the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of the body. In it he defends Christian teaching against Platonist doctrines such as the pre-existence of souls and the eternity of the world. A collection of his letters also survives.

Agapetus the Deacon was a sixth-century Byzantine cleric who served as a deacon of the church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. Tradition says he was a tutor of Justinian I, but this is uncertain. He wrote the Exposition (Capita admonitoria), seventy-two short chapters of advice addressed to Justinian around the start of his reign in 527. The first letters of the chapters spell out an acrostic dedication to the emperor. The work is an early example of the Byzantine "mirror for princes". It describes the ideal Christian ruler and was widely read and translated in later centuries.

Agathangelos ("bearer of good news") is the pseudonym under which the Armenian History of the conversion of Armenia was transmitted. The author claims to have been a secretary of King Tiridates III in the early fourth century, but the standard Armenian version dates from the second half of the fifth century. The work tells of Gregory the Illuminator's sufferings, the martyrdom of Hripsime and her companions, and the king's conversion. It also includes a long catechetical section, the Teaching of St Gregory. It is the main source for the Christianization of Armenia and survives in Greek, Arabic, Syriac, Georgian, Ethiopic and Latin versions.

Agathias Scholasticus (c. 530 – 582/594) was a Byzantine poet and historian from Myrina in Asia Minor. He worked as a lawyer in Constantinople, which is where his epithet "Scholasticus" comes from. His Histories, in five books, continue the work of Procopius. They are the main narrative source for part of Justinian I's reign, from 552 to 558, and cover wars in Italy, Lazica and against the Persians, along with digressions on Persian customs. Agathias also wrote poetry. He compiled the Cycle, an anthology of epigrams by his contemporaries, and many of his own epigrams survive in the Greek Anthology.

Agnellus (c. 487–570) was bishop of Ravenna from 557 until his death in 570, during the period of Byzantine rule in Italy after Justinian's reconquest. He oversaw the transfer of the former Arian Gothic churches of Ravenna to Catholic worship, including the rededication of the church now known as Sant'Apollinare Nuovo. He wrote a short letter to a certain Armenius, De ratione fidei, which sets out the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity against Arianism. Most of what is known about him comes from the ninth-century Liber Pontificalis of Ravenna by Andreas Agnellus, a different person with a similar name.

Agrippa Castor was a Greek Christian writer active in the reign of Hadrian, around AD 125–135. He is the earliest known writer against heresy. His work is the only recorded book written solely to refute the Alexandrian Gnostic teacher Basilides and his twenty-four books of Exegetica. The work is lost and is known mainly through Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History and Jerome. According to Eusebius, Agrippa accused Basilides of teaching that eating food offered to idols was morally indifferent and that faith could be denied under persecution. He also said Basilides imposed a five-year silence on his followers, as Pythagoras did. Nothing else is known of his life.

Ailerán, called Ailerán Sapiens ("the Wise") and in Latin Aileranus Scotus, was an Irish scholar and saint associated with the monastery of Clonard. He died on 29 December in 664 or 665, the date also kept as his feast day. He is best known for the Interpretatio mystica progenitorum Christi, an allegorical treatment of the names in Christ's genealogy, and for a moral explanation of the same names. Medieval Lives of Féchín of Fore say that he wrote an account of that saint's good works.

Airbertach mac Coise (died 1016) was an Irish scholar and poet. He served as fer léigind, or head of learning, at the monastic school of Ros Ailithir (Rosscarbery) in Munster. Irish annals record that Viking raiders carried him off in 990 and that Brian Bóruma later ransomed him. Middle Irish didactic verse is attributed to him, including a poem on the Psalms dated to 982 and a poem on the creation of Adam. Gearóid Mac Eoin suggested that he may have written Saltair na Rann, but this attribution is uncertain.

Alcuin of York (c. 735–804), also called Ealhwine or Flaccus Albinus, was an Anglo-Saxon scholar, deacon, poet and teacher. He studied at York under Archbishop Ecgbert. At Charlemagne's invitation he became a leading teacher at the Carolingian court in the 780s and 790s, and he was one of the main architects of the Carolingian Renaissance. He wrote theological and dogmatic treatises, biblical commentaries, grammatical works, letters and poems, among them question-and-answer works on the Trinity and Genesis. In 796 he became abbot of Marmoutier at Tours, where he died.

Alexander of Alexandria (died 328) was bishop of Alexandria from about 312 or 313 until his death. He dealt with disputes over the date of Easter and with the Melitian schism. He is best known for opposing Arius, the Alexandrian presbyter whom he condemned and deposed. His surviving letters on the Arian controversy include an encyclical announcing Arius's deposition and a letter to Alexander of Byzantium (or Thessalonica). He was a leading opponent of Arianism at the First Council of Nicaea in 325 and was succeeded by his deacon Athanasius. He is venerated as a saint.

Alexander of Jerusalem (died 251) was a Greek bishop of the third century. He studied at Alexandria under Pantaenus and Clement and became a lifelong friend of Origen. First a bishop in Cappadocia, he came to Jerusalem around 212 and was made coadjutor to the aged bishop Narcissus. He later succeeded him. He founded a library at Jerusalem that Eusebius later used, and he supported Origen, allowing him to preach and later ordaining him. He died in prison at Caesarea during the Decian persecution and is venerated as a martyr. Fragments of his letters survive, mostly quoted by Eusebius.

Alexander of Lycopolis was a Greek philosopher of the Platonist school who lived in Egypt in the late third century. He is known for a short treatise in twenty-six chapters against the Manichaeans. In it he defends the Platonic worldview against a new religion founded by his contemporary Mani, which missionaries had brought to Egypt. The work is an early and well-informed witness to Manichaean doctrine. Photius called him bishop of Lycopolis in the Thebaid, but since Tillemont in 1697 most scholars have held that he was a pagan.

Alexander the Monk (Alexander Monachus), often identified with Alexander of Cyprus, was a Greek monk who apparently lived in the sixth century, probably under Justinian. He is thought to have lived in the monastery near the shrine of Saint Barnabas at Salamis (Constantia) in Cyprus. Two works are attributed to him. One is a Laudatio, or encomium, of the apostle Barnabas, which recounts his mission and the finding of his relics. It also supports the Cypriot church's claim to be independent. The other is a treatise on the finding of the True Cross (De inventione crucis). His identity and exact dates remain uncertain.

Alfred the Great (c. 849–899) was King of the West Saxons from 871 and later styled King of the Anglo-Saxons. He resisted Viking invasion, winning at Edington in 878, and oversaw the baptism of the Danish leader Guthrum. He promoted learning and sponsored Old English translations of Latin works. Gregory the Great's Pastoral Care is credited to him, with a verse preface and epilogue. A version of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, including the verse Meters, is ascribed to him in its proem, though some modern scholars doubt that he was personally the author.

Alphanus of Benevento (Alphanus Beneventanus) was a Latin author in southern Italy, tentatively dated to the early seventh century, around 600–620, though this date is uncertain. He is known only as the author of a short charter in which the rights of the church of San Martino are renounced. Almost nothing else is recorded about his life or office. He should not be confused with Alfanus I, the eleventh-century archbishop of Salerno.

Ambrose Autpert (Ambrosius Autpertus, c. 730–784) was a Frankish Benedictine monk who became abbot of San Vincenzo al Volturno in southern Italy, during the reign of the Lombard king Desiderius. He wrote widely on the Bible and on spiritual subjects. His works include a major commentary on the Apocalypse, writings on the Psalms and the Song of Songs, and a life of the founders of his monastery. He also wrote the treatise on the Conflict of Vices and Virtues, which was long transmitted among the works of Augustine. Later writers honoured him for his holiness, and he has been venerated as a saint.

Ambrose (c. 339–397) was a Latin theologian and Bishop of Milan from 374 until his death. He had trained in rhetoric and law and was serving as Roman governor of Aemilia-Liguria when popular acclamation unexpectedly made him bishop. He defended Nicene orthodoxy against Arianism and excommunicated Emperor Theodosius I after a massacre. He also helped bring Greek theology to the Latin West. His writings include exegetical works such as the Exameron and the Exposition of Luke, De officiis, De Virginibus, De Sacramentis and several hymns. He influenced Augustine of Hippo and helped bring about his conversion.

Ambrosiaster, or Pseudo-Ambrose, is the name scholars give to the unknown Latin author of a commentary on the thirteen epistles of Paul. It was written between about 366 and 384, probably at Rome during the time of Pope Damasus, and was long thought to be the work of Ambrose of Milan. The name means "would-be Ambrose." Scholars have proposed several identities for the author, but none is accepted. The Quaestiones Veteris et Novi Testamenti, which was handed down under Augustine's name, is now generally assigned to the same writer. The commentary matters both for early Latin exegesis and for the Old Latin text of Paul's letters.

Ammonius of Alexandria was a Greek Christian biblical commentator. He is usually described as a presbyter of Alexandria, and his exact dates are uncertain, though he is generally placed in the late fifth or early sixth century. He should not be confused with the third-century Alexandrian Ammonius linked to a gospel harmony, or with the Neoplatonist Ammonius Saccas. None of his works survives whole. What remains are fragments of his biblical commentaries, mainly on the Gospel of John and the Acts of the Apostles, preserved in Byzantine exegetical chains (catenae). These fragments are a witness to Alexandrian exegesis after Cyril.

Amoenus was a Latin Christian poet about whom almost nothing is known. He is usually placed around the late fourth or early fifth century, though his date is uncertain. Short poems on biblical subjects survive under his name, most notably the Enchiridion Veteris et Novi Testamenti, a series of brief verse pieces on episodes from the Old and New Testaments. A few other pieces are also linked to his name, among them a poem about an Egyptian calling on the God of Martin and an acrostic addressed to a bishop Leontius of Bordeaux. Who wrote these, and when, is not settled.

Amphilochius of Iconium (c. 340 – c. 400) was a Greek bishop and theologian from a distinguished Cappadocian family, a cousin of Gregory of Nazianzus and a close friend of Basil of Caesarea, who dedicated On the Holy Spirit to him. He became bishop of Iconium around 373. He defended the divinity of the Holy Spirit, notably in a synodal letter from a council at Iconium, and he took part in the Council of Constantinople in 381. He also opposed the Messalians. His surviving works include homilies, fragments and the Iambics to Seleucus, a verse poem that contains an important list of biblical books.

Amphilochius of Side was bishop of Side in Pamphylia in the first half of the fifth century. At the Council of Ephesus (431) he strongly opposed the Messalians and signed the condemnation and deposition of Nestorius. Later he was less firm. At the Council of Chalcedon (451) he showed sympathy for Dioscorus of Alexandria and only reluctantly agreed to his condemnation, though he signed the Tome of Leo and the council's canons. In 458 he wrote to Emperor Leo I rejecting Chalcedon's authority. Only fragments of his writings survive.

Anastasius I was a Greek theologian and Chalcedonian Patriarch of Antioch. He held the see twice, from 561 to 570 or 571 and from 593 to 599. He opposed Justinian's support for Aphthartodocetism, the teaching that Christ's body could not decay, and Justin II deposed him in about 570. With the help of his friend Pope Gregory I, he was restored after Gregory of Antioch died in 593. He is credited with theological sermons and orations on orthodox faith, but some are disputed and may belong to his successor, Anastasius II. Accounts of his death in 598 or 599 also confuse the two men.

Anastasius of Sinai (Anastasius Sinaita; died after 700) was a Greek monk, priest and theologian connected with the monastery of Saint Catherine on Mount Sinai, where he is traditionally described as abbot. He wrote in the decades after the Arab conquests. His best-known work is the Viae dux (Hodegos, "Guide"), a handbook for defending Chalcedonian Christology against Monophysite opponents. Other works attributed to him include questions and answers, homilies such as the Oratio de sacra synaxi, and edifying tales about the Sinai monks. Scholars dispute some of these attributions.

Anastasius Bibliothecarius (c. 810 – c. 878/879) was a Roman cleric and scholar who knew Greek unusually well for his time. He was excommunicated under Leo IV. In 855 he briefly claimed the papacy against Benedict III but did not hold it. He was later restored to favour and served as librarian and archivist of the Holy See under Nicholas I, Adrian II and John VIII. He translated many Greek texts into Latin, including the acts of the Seventh and Eighth Ecumenical Councils, saints' lives, and the historical compilation known as the Chronographia tripartita.

Anatolius of Laodicea (died c. 283) was an Alexandrian scholar who became bishop of Laodicea in Roman Syria around 268. Eusebius praises him for his learning in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, physics and Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy. He is best known for his Paschal Canon, an early treatise on calculating the date of Easter using a nineteen-year lunar cycle. Fragments also survive of his ten books of arithmetical introductions. He is often identified with the Anatolius who taught the Neoplatonist Iamblichus, though some scholars doubt this. He is venerated as a saint, with a feast day on 3 July.

Andrew of Caesarea (563–614) was a Greek theological writer and archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Scholars once dated him anywhere from the fifth to the ninth century, but his life is now firmly placed in the late sixth and early seventh centuries. He is best known for his commentary on the Apocalypse (Revelation) of John. It is the earliest full Greek patristic commentary on that book and became the standard interpretation in the Eastern Church. It also helped win acceptance for Revelation in the Greek canon, and the many manuscripts that carry it are important for the book's textual history.

Andrew of Crete (c. 650/660–probably 740), also called Andrew of Jerusalem, was a Byzantine bishop, theologian, homilist and hymnographer. Born in Damascus, he became a monk in Jerusalem, later served as a deacon in Constantinople, and was made archbishop of Gortyna in Crete. The date of his death is disputed, with 712, 726 and 740 all proposed. His festal homilies include important sermons on the Virgin Mary. He helped establish the canon as a form of Greek hymnography. His penitential Great Canon is still sung during Great Lent. He is venerated as a saint in the Orthodox and Catholic Churches.

Andrew of Samosata (died c. 444) was bishop of Samosata on the Euphrates from about 430 and an Antiochene theologian in the Nestorian controversy. He wrote a refutation of Cyril of Alexandria's Twelve Anathemas, and much of it survives because Cyril quoted it in his reply to the Orientals. Illness kept him from the Council of Ephesus in 431. He at first opposed the 433 reunion between Cyril and John of Antioch, but around 436 he accepted it and joined in condemning Nestorius. Several of his letters about the council survive, mostly in Latin translation.

Anonymus Cyzicenus is the unnamed Greek author of a church history written around 475–480. Photius wrongly attributed it to Gelasius of Cyzicus, and the error persisted for centuries. In his preface the author says he was the son of a priest of Cyzicus and wrote in Bithynia. His purpose was to show, against the Eutychians, that the Fathers of Nicaea did not teach Monophysitism. His three-book work covers Constantine's reign, the Council of Nicaea (325) and its aftermath. It draws on earlier historians such as Rufinus and preserves documents associated with the council.

Antiochus of Saba, also called Antiochus Monachus, was a seventh-century Greek monk who is said to have been born near Ancyra. He lived first as a hermit and later became a monk of the lavra of Mar Saba near Jerusalem. He saw the Persian conquest of Palestine in 614. After Ancyra fell in 619, he wrote the Pandects of Holy Scripture for the abbot Eustathius and his displaced monks. The work is a collection of moral sayings in 130 chapters, drawn from Scripture and earlier Church writers. He also wrote the Exomologesis, a prayer lamenting Jerusalem's misfortunes. Some identify him with Strategius, who wrote an account of the sack of Jerusalem, but this has not been proven.

Antipater of Bostra was a fifth-century Greek churchman who served as metropolitan bishop of Bostra, capital of the Roman province of Arabia, in present-day southern Syria. He was active around the 450s and is remembered mainly as one of the leading critics of Origen. His chief work was a refutation of the Apology for Origen by Pamphilus and Eusebius of Caesarea, which survives only in fragments quoted by later writers. Several homilies are also attributed to him, including sermons on John the Baptist and on the Annunciation.

Anton of Tagrit, also called Antony of Tagrit or Anton the Rhetor, was a Syriac Orthodox writer active in the first half of the ninth century. He was associated with Tagrit (Tikrit) in Mesopotamia, an important centre of the West Syriac church. He is known mainly for a treatise on rhetoric that draws on the Greek rhetorical tradition, and for a theological work, On Divine Providence. These works make him an important witness to Syriac learning and to the reception of Greek literary theory under the early Abbasids.

Aphrahat, known as the Persian Sage (Latin Aphraates), was a Syriac Christian writer in the Sasanian Persian Empire. He was born in the late third century and died around 345. He was an ascetic and celibate, probably one of the "sons of the covenant", and may have been a bishop. Later tradition links him with the Mar Mattai Monastery near Mosul. His surviving work is the Demonstrations, 23 expositions on Christian faith and practice written between about 337 and 345. They cover topics including faith, prayer, asceticism and the persecution under Shapur II, and argue against Jewish teaching. They are the oldest major work of Syriac Christian literature.

Apollinaris (or Apollinarius) the Younger (c. 310 – c. 390; some accounts give 382) was bishop of Laodicea in Syria and a strong defender of Nicene orthodoxy against Arianism. With his father, Apollinaris the Elder, he recast biblical material in classical literary forms after Emperor Julian barred Christians from teaching the classics. Wanting to stress Christ's divinity and the unity of his person, he taught that the divine Logos took the place of a rational human mind in Christ. This doctrine, Apollinarism, was condemned at the First Council of Constantinople in 381. His writings survive mostly in fragments, some under the names of orthodox authors.

Apollonius was a Greek Christian writer, probably from Asia Minor, who was active in the late second and early third centuries. He wrote a treatise against the Montanists. The work itself is lost, but Eusebius quotes from it in his Ecclesiastical History, and Jerome praised it. The surviving passages attack the prophecies of Montanus and his prophetesses, including Maximilla. They also condemn the conduct of Themison and of Alexander, whom Apollonius called a false martyr. He was later described as a bishop of Ephesus, but that claim is poorly supported.

Arator (born c. 490, died after 544) was a Latin Christian poet from Liguria in northern Italy. Educated at Milan, he served at the Ostrogothic court at Ravenna before becoming a subdeacon of the Roman church. In 544 he presented his chief work, De Actibus Apostolorum, to Pope Vigilius, and it was then read publicly in Rome. The poem retells the Acts of the Apostles in two books of hexameter verse and gives the story allegorical and doctrinal interpretations. Verse letters to Florianus and to Vigilius accompany it, and it was widely read in the Middle Ages.

Arethas of Caesarea (c. 860 – c. 939) was a Byzantine churchman and scholar. He was born at Patras and became Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia early in the tenth century. He is counted among the most learned Greek theologians of his age. He wrote a commentary on the Apocalypse that draws on the earlier commentary of Andrew of Caesarea, along with scholia, letters and polemical treatises. Codices he had copied and annotated preserve important classical texts, among them works of Plato and the Meditations of Marcus Aurelius.

Aristides of Athens, also called Marcianus Aristides or Aristides the Philosopher, was a second-century Christian apologist and one of the earliest whose work survives. According to Eusebius, he presented an Apology for the Christian faith to the emperor Hadrian, though the Syriac version may be addressed to Antoninus Pius. The Apology compares the religions of barbarians, Greeks, Jews and Christians, and argues that only Christians truly know God and live rightly. Long thought lost, it was recovered in the late nineteenth century in Syriac and Armenian, and in a Greek reworking inside the romance Barlaam and Josaphat. He is venerated as a saint.

Aristo (Ariston) of Pella was a second-century Christian apologist and chronicler. Almost nothing is known of his life. Eusebius cites him as the source for Hadrian's decree, after the Bar Kokhba revolt, that barred Jews from Jerusalem, which had been refounded as Aelia Capitolina. In the seventh century Maximus the Confessor named him as the author of the lost Disputation of Jason and Papiscus. This dialogue between a Jewish Christian and an Alexandrian Jew was written around 140 and is known only from fragments and later reports. Scholars still disagree about whether Aristo wrote it.

Arnobius of Sicca (died c. 330) was an early Christian apologist from Roman North Africa, active under Diocletian. Jerome reports that he taught rhetoric at Sicca Veneria (modern El Kef, Tunisia), converted after a dream, and wrote to convince a doubtful local bishop that his faith was sincere. Jerome also names Lactantius as his pupil. His one surviving work, Adversus nationes (called Adversus gentes by Jerome), is in seven books and dates to about 303. It attacks pagan mythology and cult and defends Christianity, and it is an important source for Greco-Roman religion.

Arnobius the Younger (Arnobius Iunior) was a fifth-century Latin Christian writer, a monk or cleric who worked in Rome around the middle of the century. He may have come from Africa. He wrote an allegorical commentary on the Psalms, which Erasmus first printed in 1522 under the name of the elder Arnobius, and short notes on passages of the Gospels. He opposed Augustine's teaching on predestination, so his views have often been called semi-Pelagian. The Conflictus de Deo trino et uno has sometimes been ascribed to him, but this is disputed. Some scholars also credit him with the Passio of Saint Cecilia.

Arsen II was Catholicos of Kartli, head of the Georgian Church, from about 955 to 980. He is remembered as a hagiographer. His surviving work is a Life of John of Zedazeni, the leader of the Thirteen Assyrian Fathers, who were monks traditionally said to have come from Syria in the sixth century to promote monasticism in Georgia. The Life survives in several redactions. Arsen's writing belongs to the growth of Georgian church literature in the tenth century, when native saints' lives were being written and revised.

Arsenius the Great (c. 350/354 – c. 445/450), also called Arsenius the Deacon or the Roman, was one of the most revered Desert Fathers. Tradition holds that he was a Roman of senatorial rank who tutored the sons of Emperor Theodosius I before he withdrew to Egypt. There he lived as an anchorite at Scetis and later at Troe (Turah) near Memphis. He was known for his strict silence, his flight from human company and his gift of tears. His sayings hold a prominent place in the Apophthegmata Patrum. A few short ascetic instructions are also attributed to him.

Asterius of Amasea (c. 350 – c. 410) was a Greek Christian bishop and preacher. Born in Cappadocia, he worked as a lawyer before becoming bishop of Amasea in Pontus, sometime between 380 and 390. A substantial number of his lively homilies survive. They are valued for what they show of social life in late antiquity and for art history, notably his description of a painting of the martyrdom of Saint Euphemia, which the Second Council of Nicaea cited in 787. He is distinct from the Arian writer Asterius the Sophist. His feast day is 30 October.

Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–298 – 373), called "the Great", was an Egyptian theologian and the twentieth bishop of Alexandria, serving from 328 until his death. As a deacon he went with Bishop Alexander to the Council of Nicaea in 325. He then spent his career defending the Nicene faith against Arianism. His conflicts with Arian churchmen and with successive emperors led to five exiles. His writings include On the Incarnation, the Orations against the Arians, the Letters to Serapion on the Holy Spirit and the Life of Antony. He is honoured as one of the four Great Greek Church Fathers.

Athenagoras was a Greek Christian apologist of the second half of the 2nd century. Little is known of his life beyond his being an Athenian philosopher who converted to Christianity. His Plea for the Christians (Legatio), addressed around 177 to the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus, answers the charges of atheism, cannibalism and incest brought against Christians. It is notable for its philosophical defence of monotheism and its early account of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. A treatise On the Resurrection of the Dead is also attributed to him, though some scholars dispute his authorship. The Eastern Orthodox Church commemorates him on 24 July.

Atticus (died 10 October 425) was archbishop of Constantinople from March 406 until his death. He opposed John Chrysostom and helped bring about his deposition. As bishop he rebuilt the small church on the site of the later Hagia Sophia. He also opposed the Pelagians, which made him more popular in the city. His teaching added to the theological basis of the growing devotion to the Virgin Mary. Only a letter and some fragments of his writings survive. Sisinnius I succeeded him after a period in which the see stood vacant.

Augustine of Canterbury (died c. 604 or 605) was a Roman monk and the first Archbishop of Canterbury. He was prior of a monastery in Rome when Pope Gregory I chose him in 595 to lead a mission to the Anglo-Saxons. He landed in Kent in 597, and King Æthelberht converted and gave him land at Canterbury, where he founded the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul, later St Augustine's Abbey. He set up sees at London and Rochester but failed to win over the British bishops. Very little writing by him survives, and documents later attributed to him are of doubtful authenticity.

Augustine of Hippo (354–430) was a Latin theologian and philosopher. He was born at Thagaste in Roman North Africa and became bishop of Hippo Regius. As a young man he followed Manichaeism and then Neoplatonism. Ambrose baptised him in Milan in 386. He wrote against Manichaeans, Donatists and Pelagians, and his teaching on grace, original sin and the sacraments shaped Western theology. His major works include the Confessions, an early spiritual autobiography, along with The City of God, On the Trinity and On Christian Doctrine. He is honoured as a saint and Doctor of the Church.

Augustine the Irishman (Augustinus Hibernicus) was an Irish monk and exegete of the mid-seventh century. Little is known of his life. He wrote De mirabilibus sacrae Scripturae, a treatise in three books dated to about 654–655. It explains the miracles of the Old and New Testaments as far as possible in terms of the natural order God established at creation, rather than as new creations. The work was long transmitted among the writings of Augustine of Hippo. It is an important witness to Irish learning and biblical scholarship in the early Middle Ages.

Aunarius (also Aunacharius, French Aunaire) was bishop of Auxerre in Merovingian Gaul in the later sixth century. He was born around 540 and died around 603 or 605; the exact dates of his life and episcopate are uncertain. He is venerated as a saint. Aunarius presided over the diocesan synod of Auxerre, held around 585, whose canons deal with church discipline, liturgy and the survival of pagan customs. He also encouraged devotion to his predecessor Germanus of Auxerre. A surviving letter of his is addressed to an abbot named Stephen, whom he asked to write about the saints of Auxerre.

Aurelian (Aurelianus) was bishop of Arles in southern Gaul from 546 until his death in 551. He followed Auxanius and stood in the tradition of Caesarius of Arles. His father Sacerdos was bishop of Lyon, and Aurelian died at Lyon on 16 June 551, where he was buried; his epitaph survives. With the support of the Frankish king Childebert I he founded a monastery for men and a convent for women at Arles. For them he wrote two monastic rules, drawing heavily on Caesarius's rules. A letter he sent to King Theudebert also survives in part.

Aurelius of Carthage (died c. 430) was bishop of Carthage and primate of the African church from about 391 until his death, and is venerated as a saint. A close friend and ally of Augustine of Hippo, he presided over many of the councils of Carthage. These councils regulated church discipline, opposed Donatism and condemned Pelagianism. His surviving writings are mostly synodal and circular letters to bishops issued in connection with these councils. A letter to Pope Damasus that bears his name is spurious, because Damasus died in 384, several years before Aurelius became bishop.

Decimus Magnus Ausonius (c. 310 – c. 395) was a Latin poet and teacher of rhetoric from Burdigala (Bordeaux) in Aquitaine. He taught for many years in his native city and was then called to the imperial court as tutor to the future emperor Gratian, who later made him consul in 379. His best-known poems are the Mosella, a description of the River Moselle, and the Ephemeris, an account of a typical day. Other works, such as the Parentalia, commemorate his family, teachers and friends. He corresponded with his former pupil Paulinus of Nola and is counted among the Christian writers of late antiquity.

Auspicius of Toul (Latin Auspicius Tullensis) was a fifth-century bishop of Toul in Gaul. He is traditionally counted as the fifth recorded holder of the see and is venerated as a saint. He was active around 470–475 and may have died around 490. His surviving work is a verse letter written about 470 to Arbogast, count of Trier. It praises Arbogast's learning and Christian virtue and urges him to remain generous to the Church. The poem is notable for its iambic lines built on stress accent rather than classical syllable length, an early example of rhythmic Latin verse.

Autbert, also called Aubert, was bishop of Cambrai and Arras in the seventh century. He held the see from about 633 until his death in 669. He is venerated as a saint and is remembered for encouraging monastic life in his diocese, in the Frankish territories of northern Gaul. A Latin charter about a monastery called Wallarensis survives under his name, as is common for Merovingian episcopal documents. Little else is securely known of his writings.

Avitus of Braga (Avitus Bracarensis) was a priest from Braga in Roman Gallaecia, now northern Portugal, who was in Palestine in the early fifth century. He was there during the Pelagian controversy around 415, and he had links with Augustine and with his fellow Bracaran Paulus Orosius. He is remembered for translating into Latin the Greek account by the priest Lucian of how Saint Stephen's tomb was found in 415. He prefaced the translation with a letter to Palchonius of Braga and entrusted relics of Stephen to Orosius to carry home. Orosius left the relics on Minorca, and they never reached Braga.

Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus (c. 450 – 517/518 or 519) was a Latin poet and bishop of Vienne in Burgundian Gaul. He came from a prominent Gallo-Roman senatorial family related to the Emperor Avitus. As bishop he opposed Arianism and helped bring the Burgundian prince Sigismund to Catholic Christianity. He also served as a kind of secretary to the Burgundian kings. His surviving writings include nearly a hundred letters, which are an important source for the politics and theology of his time. His best-known poem, De spiritalis historiae gestis, retells biblical history from the Creation to the Exodus in five books of hexameters.

Bachiarius was a Latin Christian writer of the late fourth and early fifth centuries. Almost nothing is known of his life except what his two surviving works suggest: he seems to have been a monk from Galicia in the Iberian Peninsula. In his Professio fidei he defends his own orthodoxy, apparently against suspicions raised by his origins at a time when Priscillianism was strong in that region. His Liber de reparatione lapsi argues that a monk who had sinned with a consecrated virgin could be restored through penance.

Balai was a Syriac poet of the early fifth century, active around Qenneshrin (Chalcis) in northern Syria. Tradition describes him as a chorepiscopus in the region of Beroea (Aleppo). Little is known of his life; he may have come from Edessa. His surviving works include five madroshe on Bishop Acacius of Beroea, who died in 436, and a madrosho for the dedication of a church at Qenneshrin. Twelve memre on Joseph are attributed both to him and to Ephrem, and scholars disagree over who wrote them. The five-syllable Syriac metre is traditionally named after him.

Bardaisan (Latin Bardesanes; 154–222) was a Syriac-speaking Christian teacher, philosopher, astrologer and poet at Edessa, capital of the kingdom of Osroene. Later writers regarded him as a heretic, and he founded a school known as the Bardaisanites. Eusebius reports that he once followed the Gnostic Valentinus but later opposed him, and he also wrote against Marcion. His hymns and a book on India are lost. The Book of the Laws of Countries, a dialogue on fate, nature and free will written down by his disciple Philip, preserves his teaching.

Barlaha was a Syriac Christian writer known only as the author of a letter addressed to a certain Simeon, which is preserved in the Syriac literary tradition. The letter's subject is described differently in different places, either as the translation of the Psalms or as the translation (transfer) of relics. Nothing certain is known of Barlaha's life, office or location, and his date is undetermined.

Barnabas, born Joseph or Joses, was a Cypriot Levite and a leading figure in the earliest Jerusalem church. Acts calls him an apostle. He was a companion of Paul the Apostle on missionary journeys among Gentiles in Anatolia and took part in the Council of Jerusalem around 49. He left no writings that can be shown to be his own. Early writers, including Clement of Alexandria, credited him with the Epistle of Barnabas, and Tertullian named him as author of Hebrews. Most modern scholars reject both attributions. Tradition holds that he was martyred at Salamis in Cyprus and regards him as founder of the Cypriot church.

Barsanuphius of Gaza, also called Barsanuphius the Great, was a sixth-century Christian hermit and one of the Desert Fathers. He was an enclosed recluse at the monastery of Seridus near Gaza in Palestine and died sometime after 543. Barsanuphius and his fellow recluse John the Prophet gave spiritual guidance to monks, clergy and lay people by letter. More than 850 of their questions and answers survive, and they strongly influenced Orthodox monasticism. Some of the replies deal with the controversy over the teachings of Origen and Evagrius. Both the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches venerate him as a saint.

Bartholomew of Edessa was a Christian monk and polemical writer who wrote in Greek. In his refutation he calls himself "the monk of Edessa" several times, so he was probably born in or near that city. Little else is known about his life. His date is disputed: estimates range from the ninth to the thirteenth century, and recent scholarship tends to place him in the thirteenth. He is known for the Elenchus et confutatio Agareni, an apologetic treatise against Islam. It defends Christian doctrine and attacks Muslim teaching and the prophet Muhammad.

Basil II (958–1025), called the Bulgar-Slayer, was senior Byzantine emperor from 976 to 1025, the longest reign of any Roman emperor. He was crowned as a child but only began to rule in person after removing his great-uncle Basil Lekapenos in 985. He put down the revolts of Bardas Skleros and Bardas Phokas, expanded the eastern frontier and, after a long war, fully conquered the First Bulgarian Empire. His legislation (novels), notably the novel of 996, limited the power of the great landowning families. He left the empire with a full treasury and at its greatest extent in four centuries.

Basil of Ancyra (died c. 364) was a Greek bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, appointed in 336 in place of the deposed Marcellus, and said to have been a physician by training. In the doctrinal disputes after Nicaea he led the "homoiousian" party, which held that the Son is "of like substance" with the Father. He played a prominent part at the Council of Ancyra in 358. He was deposed at Constantinople in 360 and sent into exile. A treatise On Virginity, long preserved among the works of Basil of Caesarea, is attributed to him.

Basil of Caesarea, called Basil the Great (c. 330–379), was a Greek church father and bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia from 370 until his death. With his brother Gregory of Nyssa and his friend Gregory of Nazianzus he is counted among the Cappadocian Fathers. He defended Nicene orthodoxy against Arianism, and his treatise On the Holy Spirit helped shape Trinitarian doctrine. His monastic rules became the basis of communal monasticism in the East. He is also known for his Hexaemeron, his homilies and letters, the liturgy that bears his name, and the Basileias, a charitable foundation for the poor and sick.

Basil of Neopatras (Latin Basilius Neopatrensis) was a Byzantine Greek churchman associated with the see of Neopatras in central Greece. His dates are uncertain, though he is usually placed in the first half of the tenth century. He is known for a prologue to an interpretation of the twelve Minor Prophets. This was an introduction to the exegesis of those books, of the kind found in Byzantine commentary collections. Little else is reliably known of his life or other writings.

Basil of Seleucia (died c. 468) was a Greek bishop and church writer of the fifth century. He was archbishop of Seleucia ad Calycadnum in Isauria by 448. His record in the Christological disputes was uneven. In 448 he condemned Eutyches. At the Second Council of Ephesus (the "Latrocinium") in 449 he went along with Eutyches' rehabilitation, but he later recanted and signed the Tome of Leo. A collection of his sermons, the Orationes, survives. The Life and Miracles of Saint Thecla was long attributed to him, but it is now considered the work of an anonymous contemporary.

Basil of Zarzma (Basili Zarzmeli) was a Georgian monk and hagiographer, probably of the tenth century. He was associated with the monastery of Zarzma in Samtskhe, southwest Georgia. He wrote the Life of Serapion of Zarzma, an account of the monk who founded Zarzma in the ninth century. The work is a significant early piece of Georgian hagiography. It is also a source for the monastic movement in southern Georgia and for the region's history in this period. Little else is securely known about his life.

Basil the Minor (Basilius Minimus), also called Basil the Younger, was a Byzantine churchman and scholiast active in the mid-tenth century. He is generally identified as a metropolitan of Caesarea in Cappadocia. He is known for his scholia on the orations of Gregory of Nazianzus, which explain the orator's difficult language, allusions and theological points. Tradition holds that he dedicated the commentary to Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus. His notes were often handed down with other explanatory material on Gregory, such as the mythological commentaries attributed to Pseudo-Nonnus.

Beccán mac Luigdech was a seventh-century Irish monk and hermit linked to the monastic community of Iona. He wrote two Old Irish poems praising Columba (Colum Cille), Iona's founder: Fo réir Choluimb ("Bound to Colum") and Tiugraind Beccáin ("The last verses of Beccán"). Both are usually dated to around 640. With the Amra Choluim Cille and Adomnán's Life of Columba, they give an early view of Iona's monastic family. He is usually identified with the hermit Beccán who received Cummian's letter on the Easter controversy (c. 632–33). He may also be the Beccán of Rum whose death the Annals of Ulster record in 677.

Bede (672/3–735), known as the Venerable Bede, was a Northumbrian monk and scholar of the twin monastery of Monkwearmouth–Jarrow, where he spent almost his whole life. One of the most important writers of the early Middle Ages, he is best known for his Ecclesiastical History of the English People. He also wrote many biblical commentaries and works on computus, the reckoning of the calendar and of Easter, and helped spread the practice of dating years Anno Domini. A short Old English poem, known as Bede's Death Song, is traditionally attributed to him on his deathbed.

Benedict of Nursia (c. 480 – c. 547) was an Italian monk often regarded as the founder of Western Christian monasticism. According to tradition, he first lived as a hermit and then founded twelve monastic communities at Subiaco, east of Rome. He later moved to Monte Cassino, where he established the monastery tied to his name. His Rule for monks draws on John Cassian and is closely related to the earlier Rule of the Master. It is known for its balance and moderation, and it became the dominant monastic rule of the medieval West. Most of what is known about his life comes from the Dialogues of Gregory the Great.

Berengaudus is the name given to the author of the Expositio super septem visiones libri Apocalypsis, a Latin commentary on the Book of Revelation that reads the book as seven visions. Tradition makes him a Benedictine monk of Ferrières Abbey in the ninth century, in the time of Lupus Servatus. However, both his identity and his date are disputed, and some scholars place the work in the eleventh or twelfth century. The commentary circulated widely from the twelfth century onward. It was once printed among the works of Ambrose. In Old French translation it accompanied many English Gothic illuminated Apocalypse manuscripts.

Bertram of Le Mans (Bertechramnus; died 623) was a Frankish bishop of Le Mans from 586 or 587 until his death. He was one of the wealthiest churchmen of Merovingian Gaul. With Namatius of Orléans he served King Guntram as an envoy to the Bretons. He is best known for his Testamentum, a long will dated 616. It lists estates covering more than 3,000 square kilometres and gifts to churches and monasteries. The will is an important source for landholding, the Church and society in early seventh-century Gaul.

Besa was a Coptic monk of fifth-century Upper Egypt. He was a disciple of Shenoute of Atripe and succeeded him as head of the White Monastery near Sohag, probably around the middle of the century. His surviving letters and sermons, written in Sahidic Coptic, are addressed to the monks and nuns of the community. They deal with discipline, obedience, repentance and disputes within the monastery, and they show how Shenoute's monastic rule was kept up after his death. Tradition also attributes to Besa the Life of Shenoute, though his authorship of it is debated.

Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524) was a Roman senator, consul and philosopher who served under the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great. He was born in Rome into the Anicii family and raised by Symmachus. He set out to translate and comment on the Greek philosophical classics in Latin, and produced commentaries on Porphyry and Aristotle along with treatises on logic, music, arithmetic and theology. These included the Theological Tractates on the Trinity and the Catholic faith. Accused of treason, he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison before his execution. It became one of the most influential books of the Middle Ages.

Bovo (died 916), sometimes called Bovo II, was abbot of the Benedictine monastery of Corvey in Saxony from about 900 until his death. He is remembered as a scholar for his Latin commentary on the ninth metre of Book III of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, the hymn "O qui perpetua". In it he explains the poem's cosmological and philosophical teaching but warns that some of its ideas, such as the pre-existence of souls, come from Platonist philosophy rather than Christian doctrine. The commentary is an important witness to how early medieval readers received Boethius.

Braulio (c. 585–651) was bishop of Zaragoza in Visigothic Hispania from about 631, succeeding his brother John. He was a close friend and correspondent of Isidore of Seville. After Isidore's death he edited the Etymologiae and wrote the Renotatio, a list of Isidore's works. He took part in the councils of Toledo and was one of the leading churchmen and writers of his time. His surviving letters are a valuable source for the period. He also wrote a Life of Saint Aemilian (Millán), the hermit of La Rioja. He is venerated as a saint.

Bulgaranus, also called Bulgar, was a Visigothic count active around 610–612, during the reign of King Gundemar. He seems to have held office in the Visigothic territories bordering Frankish Gaul, probably Septimania. He is known for a small group of Latin letters addressed to bishops in Francia, preserved among the letters of the Visigothic period. They deal with relations between the Visigothic kingdom and the Frankish realms, and they show how a lay official in seventh-century Spain wrote letters in Latin and dealt with church leaders.

Cædmon (fl. c. 657–680) is the earliest English poet whose name is known. He was a Northumbrian cowherd at the double monastery of Streonæshalch (Whitby) while Hild was abbess. Bede's Ecclesiastical History tells how Cædmon, who had no skill in song, received the gift of composing verse in a dream. He then entered the monastery and turned passages of Scripture into Old English poetry. His only surviving work is Cædmon's Hymn, a short alliterative poem praising God the Creator and one of the oldest recorded examples of Old English verse. He is venerated as a saint.

Caesarius of Arles (c. 470–542) was the leading churchman of Merovingian Gaul. Born at Chalon-sur-Saône, he became a monk at Lérins and was bishop of Arles from 502 until his death. He was deeply influenced by Augustine, Julianus Pomerius and John Cassian, and was famous as a tireless popular preacher. His large body of short Latin sermons, mostly on moral instruction, was widely copied and reused. He founded a convent for women at Arles and wrote a rule for its nuns. He also presided over the Council of Orange (529), which affirmed Augustinian teaching on grace.

Caesarius of Nazianzus (c. 331–368/369) was a Cappadocian physician and imperial official, and the younger brother of Gregory of Nazianzus. He studied in Alexandria and became a court physician in Constantinople. Under Julian he stayed true to his Christian faith and left the court. Later, under Valens, he held a financial office in Bithynia. He survived the earthquake at Nicaea in 368 and died soon afterwards. Gregory's funeral oration for him is the main source for his life. He is venerated as a saint. A collection of questions and answers on theology that circulates under his name is a later work by an unknown author ("Pseudo-Caesarius").

Caius (or Gaius) was a learned Roman presbyter active in the early third century, under Pope Zephyrinus. He is distinct from the later Pope Caius. He wrote in Greek and is known mainly for his Dialogue against Proclus, a defender of Montanism. Eusebius preserved fragments of it, including the famous reference to the "trophies" of the apostles Peter and Paul on the Vatican hill and the Ostian Way. Later sources say he rejected the Johannine Apocalypse and ascribed it to Cerinthus. Some ancient writers attributed the Little Labyrinth to him, but this attribution is doubtful.

Candidus the Arian is a Latin writer known only from his exchange with the Roman rhetorician and theologian Marius Victorinus, around the late 350s. Two texts survive under his name. One is a treatise on the divine generation, which argues that God is unbegotten and unchangeable, so the Son cannot be begotten from the Father's substance. The other is a letter to Victorinus that includes Latin versions of letters by Arius and Eusebius of Nicomedia. Victorinus wrote anti-Arian replies to him. Many scholars think Candidus was a literary fiction that Victorinus created to present the opposing view.

Candidus the Isaurian (fl. late fifth century) was an Eastern Roman historian who wrote in Greek. He came from Isauria and is said to have served as a secretary to powerful Isaurian leaders. His history, in three books, covered events from the accession of Leo I in 457 to the accession of Anastasius I in 491. It dealt in particular with the reign of the Isaurian emperor Zeno. The work is lost and survives only in fragments and in a summary in Photius's Bibliotheca. It remains a valuable source for Eastern Roman politics in this period.

Capreolus was bishop of Carthage and primate of the African Church from about 430 until his death around 437, succeeding Aurelius. He led the church as the Vandals were invading Roman Africa. The Vandal invasion kept him from attending the Council of Ephesus in 431, so he sent his deacon Besulas with a letter. The letter was read at the council and urged it to keep to established doctrine and reject new teachings. His surviving Latin letters also include one to Vitalis and Constantius on the two natures of Christ, opposing Nestorian views.

Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator (c. 485 – c. 585) was a Roman statesman and scholar. He served in high office under Theodoric the Great and his successors in Ostrogothic Italy. His official letters were collected in the Variae, and he also wrote a Chronicle and a now-lost History of the Goths. In later life he turned to Christian learning and founded the monastery of Vivarium in Calabria. There he encouraged the copying of manuscripts and wrote the Institutiones, a guide to sacred and secular study, along with a long commentary on the Psalms.

Castor of Apt was bishop of Apt, in Provence in southern Gaul, in the early fifth century. He died in the 420s, though sources disagree on whether it was about 423 or 426. He is honoured as a saint, and Nîmes Cathedral is dedicated partly to him. He is best known for his link to John Cassian. At Castor's request, Cassian wrote the Institutes, a guide to monastic life for a monastery Castor wanted to found, and dedicated the Institutes and the first Conferences to him. A short letter to Cassian has come down under Castor's name.

Cerealis was a Catholic bishop of Castellum in Roman North Africa, probably in Mauretania, in the late fifth century, under the Arian Vandal kingdom. He is linked to the persecution under King Huneric, when Catholic bishops were summoned to Carthage in 484. He is known as the author of a short Latin treatise against an Arian named Maximinus. In it he answers questions about the Trinity by gathering passages of Scripture that support the full divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Ceretius was bishop of Grenoble in Gaul in the mid-fifth century, and little is known of his life. His surviving writing is a letter to Pope Leo the Great, written around 450–451 together with the Gallic bishops Salonius and Veranus. In it the bishops thank Leo for his doctrinal letter to Flavian of Constantinople, the Tome, which set out the doctrine of Christ's two natures against Eutyches. They had received and read it, and they ask the pope to correct their copy if necessary. The letter shows that Gallic bishops followed and supported Rome in the Christological controversy before the Council of Chalcedon.

Childebert I (c. 496–558) was a Frankish king of the Merovingian dynasty. He was the son of Clovis I and Saint Clotilde and was born at Reims. When his father's kingdom was divided in 511, he became King of Paris, and from 524 he also ruled Orléans. Together with his brothers he fought the Burgundians and the Visigoths. He supported the Church and is remembered for founding the Parisian abbey later known as Saint-Germain-des-Prés. A short Latin royal decree is preserved under his name. It orders the destruction of pagan idols and the suppression of surviving pagan practices in his realm.

Chlothar I (c. 497–561), sometimes called "the Old", was a Merovingian king of the Franks and one of the four sons of Clovis I and Queen Clotilde. When his father's kingdom was divided in 511, he received a share. He spent much of his reign expanding his lands at the expense of neighbouring peoples and his own relatives. After outliving his brothers, he reunited Francia under his sole rule in 558. On his death the kingdom was again divided among his sons. A royal legal decree, the Constitutio Generalis, is attributed to him, though some scholars assign it to Chlothar II.

Chlothar II (584–629) was a Merovingian king of the Franks and the son of Chilperic I and Fredegund. He became king of Neustria as an infant, with his mother as regent, and took power himself after her death in 597. In 613 he defeated Queen Brunhilda and had her executed, which made him ruler of all Francia. His Edict of Paris (614) followed a church council held in that city and dealt with appointments to office and the running of the kingdom. He generally supported the church. In 617 he made the office of mayor of the palace a post held for life, and in 623 he gave Austrasia to his son Dagobert I.

Chernorizets Hrabar ("Hrabar the Monk") was a Bulgarian monk and writer who lived in the First Bulgarian Empire around 900, during the reign of Tsar Simeon. Nothing certain is known of his life, and scholars have debated whether "Hrabar" is a real name or a pseudonym. He is linked with the Preslav Literary School. He is known as the author of On the Letters. This treatise defends the Slavonic alphabet created by Constantine-Cyril and Methodius against critics who held that only Hebrew, Greek and Latin were fit for Scripture and worship.

Christopher of Alexandria (Christophorus Alexandrinus, died 841) was the Melkite, or Greek Orthodox, Patriarch of Alexandria from about 817 until his death. He led the Chalcedonian church in Egypt under Abbasid rule during the second period of Byzantine Iconoclasm. He is traditionally named, together with Job of Antioch and Basil of Jerusalem, as one of the authors of the Letter of the Three Patriarchs (836). This letter to Emperor Theophilos defended the veneration of icons. A small body of Greek encomia and short writings is also attributed to him.

Chromatius (died c. 406/407) was bishop of Aquileia in northeastern Italy from about 388. He was probably born and raised in Aquileia, and before becoming bishop he served as a priest there. He was a friend and patron of Jerome and of Rufinus. Jerome dedicated several biblical translations to him, and Rufinus translated Eusebius's Church History at his request. He tried to make peace between the two men during their bitter quarrel. He is known for his Latin sermons and his tractates on the Gospel of Matthew, which include an exposition of the Beatitudes.

Claudianus Ecdidius Mamertus (died c. 473/474) was a Gallo-Roman theologian and philosopher. He was a priest at Vienne and the younger brother of Saint Mamertus, the city's bishop. A friend of Sidonius Apollinaris, he was admired for his learning. His chief work, De statu animae, in three books, defends the incorporeal nature of the human soul against the view of Faustus of Riez that it is corporeal. It draws on Augustine and Neoplatonic thought. A few of his letters also survive.

Claudius Apollinaris, also called Apollinaris of Hierapolis or Apollinaris the Apologist, was bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia in the later second century, active around 165–180. Eusebius lists his writings. They include an apology addressed to the emperor Marcus Aurelius, works titled Against the Greeks, On Truth and Against the Jews, and treatises against the Montanist movement, which arose in Phrygia during his lifetime. Almost all of this is lost. Surviving fragments include passages on the date of Easter, preserved in the Chronicon Paschale, that bear on the Quartodeciman controversy. He is venerated as a saint.

Claudius Mamertinus was a Roman official and Latin orator of the mid-to-late fourth century. In late 361 he sat on the Chalcedon tribunal that tried the ministers of Constantius II. The emperor Julian rewarded him with the consulship for 362. On 1 January of that year, in Constantinople, he delivered the Gratiarum Actio, a speech thanking Julian for the office, which survives in the Panegyrici Latini. He later served as praetorian prefect of Italy, Africa and Illyricum and was removed from office in 368 on charges of embezzlement.

Claudius Marius Victorius, also called Victor or Victorinus, was a Latin rhetor, meaning a teacher of rhetoric and a poet, at Marseille in southern Gaul. He was active in the first half of the fifth century and died around 425–450. His main work is the Alethia ("Truth"), a hexameter poem in three books that retells and comments on Genesis, from the Creation to the story of Abraham. It belongs to the tradition of Latin biblical epic. A letter to an abbot named Salomon, attacking the moral corruption of his age, is also attributed to him.

Clement of Alexandria (Titus Flavius Clemens, c. 150 – c. 215) was a Greek Christian theologian and philosopher. A convert educated in classical philosophy and literature, he taught at the Catechetical School of Alexandria, where Origen and Alexander of Jerusalem were among his pupils. His three major works form a trilogy: the Protrepticus (Exhortation to the Greeks), the Paedagogus (Instructor) and the Stromata (Miscellanies). He also wrote the treatise Who is the Rich Man that Shall be Saved? Clement drew heavily on Plato and the Stoics and presented Christianity as the true gnosis, fulfilling Greek philosophy.

Clement of Rome (Clemens Romanus, died c. 100), also counted as Pope Clement I, was bishop of Rome in the late first century and is traditionally regarded as the first of the Apostolic Fathers. Early lists name him the second, third or fourth bishop of Rome, and Irenaeus says he knew the apostles. Little is known for certain about his life. Later legend says he was exiled and martyred under Trajan. His only writing generally accepted as genuine is the First Epistle to the Corinthians (c. 96). In it he urged the Corinthian church to restore presbyters it had deposed, appealing to the authority the apostles gave to church leaders.

Clovis I (Latin Chlodovechus, c. 466–511) was king of the Franks and is regarded as the founder of the Merovingian dynasty. He succeeded his father Childeric I in 481 and joined the Frankish kingdoms under one ruler. He defeated Syagrius at Soissons in 486, subdued the Alemanni, and conquered Visigothic Aquitaine after the battle of Vouillé in 507. Influenced by his wife Clotilde, he was baptized a Catholic sometime between 498 and 506, rather than becoming an Arian. His conversion shaped the religious future of Gaul. A short letter to the bishops, issued after the Gothic war, survives under his name.

Cogitosus was an Irish monk active in the mid-to-late seventh century, probably connected with the monastery of Kildare. He wrote the Latin Vita Sanctae Brigidae, the earliest surviving life of Brigid of Kildare. The Life is mainly an account of her miracles. It also promotes Kildare's status and gives a notable description of its large church, which housed the tombs of Brigid and Bishop Conlaed. Muirchú, the hagiographer of Patrick, refers to Cogitosus as his predecessor in writing saints' lives. Little else is known about him.

Colmán maccu Béognae, also called Colmán Elo or Colmán of Lynally, was an Irish abbot and saint who died in 611. He founded the monastery of Lann Elo (Lynally, in present-day County Offaly) and is remembered as one of the leading churchmen of early Irish monasticism. Tradition ascribes to him the Apgitir Chrábaid ("Alphabet of Piety"), an Old Irish prose guide to the ascetic and devotional life, and one of the earliest surviving works of Irish religious prose. Scholars dispute the attribution, though Pádraig Ó Néill has argued in favour of it.

Columbanus (543–615), also called Columba the Younger, was an Irish monk and missionary. He was trained in Ireland, notably at Bangor, and travelled to the continent around 590. There he founded monasteries in the Frankish and Lombard kingdoms, most famously Luxeuil in Burgundy and Bobbio in northern Italy. He is one of the earliest identifiable Hiberno-Latin writers. His works include monastic rules, a penitential that promoted private confession followed by penances set by a priest, sermons (Instructiones) and letters. His foundations spread Irish monastic practice widely across early medieval Europe.

Commodian (Commodianus) was a Christian Latin poet. His date is disputed, with proposals ranging from the mid-third to the fifth century. He is usually thought to have come from Roman Africa, though a Syrian origin has also been suggested. By his own account he was a pagan who converted late in life. He wrote the Instructiones, eighty acrostic poems that mock pagan gods and admonish Jews and Christians, and the Carmen Apologeticum, which covers salvation history and the end times. Both are written in an early accentual (rhythmic) hexameter. His millenarian views led the Gelasian Decree to class his works as apocryphal.

Constantine Leichoudes (died 1063) was a Byzantine statesman and Patriarch of Constantinople from 1059 to 1063, reigning as Constantine III. Before he was ordained, he was a leading official at the imperial court under Constantine IX Monomachos. He belonged to the circle of learned men around Michael Psellos, who later wrote a funeral oration in his honour. He became patriarch after Michael Keroularios was removed under Isaac I Komnenos. Some of the canonical decrees and letters he issued as patriarch survive.

Constantine the Deacon was a Greek ecclesiastical writer and a deacon of the church of Constantinople. Almost nothing is known of his life, and his date is uncertain; he is usually placed in the sixth or seventh century. He is known as the author of an encomium in praise of all the martyrs, the Laudatio omnium martyrum. This homily celebrates the martyrs of the Church together and reflects the Byzantine cult of the martyrs and the rhetoric of festal preaching in Constantinople.

Constantine I, known as Constantine the Great (c. 272–337), was Roman emperor from 306 to 337. He was born at Naissus, and his army proclaimed him emperor at York. He defeated his rivals Maxentius and Licinius and in 324 became sole ruler of the empire. He was the first emperor to adopt Christianity. With Licinius he issued the Edict of Milan (313), which ended the persecution of Christians. He called the Council of Nicaea and founded Constantinople. Several letters, laws and an Oration to the Assembly of the Saints survive under his name. He was baptized shortly before his death.

Constantine V (718–775) was Byzantine emperor from 741 to 775, son and successor of Leo III. He was an able military leader who campaigned against the Arabs and fought repeated wars against the Bulgars in the Balkans, and he carried out important military and administrative reforms. A fervent iconoclast and opponent of monasticism, he summoned the Council of Hieria (754) against the veneration of images. He wrote theological treatises on the subject, known from later refutations. The Ecloga law code was issued in his and his father's joint names. Later Byzantine writers vilified him as "Kopronymos".

Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (905–959) was Byzantine emperor of the Macedonian dynasty, the son of Leo VI and Zoe Karbonopsina. He reigned nominally from 913, first under his mother's regency and then alongside Romanos Lekapenos and his sons, before ruling alone from 945. He was a patron of learning and a major figure of Byzantine encyclopaedism. Works written or compiled under his name include De administrando imperio, a policy manual for his son Romanos II, De cerimoniis on court ritual, and De thematibus on the provinces. His authorship of the Vita Basilii is uncertain.

Cosmas Indicopleustes ("who sailed to India") was a sixth-century Greek-speaking merchant and traveller from Alexandria. During the reign of Justinian he made voyages to the Kingdom of Aksum and the Indian Ocean region, and later in life he seems to have taken up a retired, possibly monastic, life. He followed the Church of the East and was a pupil of the future patriarch Aba I. He wrote the Christian Topography around 550. It describes a flat, tabernacle-shaped universe based on Scripture, but it also preserves valuable observations about trade, peoples, animals and Christian communities in India, Ceylon and Ethiopia, along with some of the earliest surviving world maps.

Cosmas of Maiuma was an eighth-century Greek hymnographer and bishop, also called Cosmas of Jerusalem, Cosmas Hagiopolites ("of the Holy City") or Cosmas the Melodist. By tradition he was the foster brother of John of Damascus, and both were taught by the monk Cosmas the Sicilian. He is said to have been a monk at the Lavra of Saint Sabas before becoming bishop of Maiuma, the port of Gaza. He died in 773 or 794. He is best known for his liturgical canons for major feasts, still sung in the Byzantine rite. He is traditionally identified with the scholiast who explained the historical allusions in Gregory of Nazianzus's poems. He is venerated as a saint.

Cosmas Vestitor was a Byzantine Greek homilist whose exact dates are uncertain. He is usually placed somewhere between the mid-eighth and mid-ninth centuries. His byname refers to the court title vestitor, an imperial wardrobe official, which suggests he was a layman serving at court. He is known for festal sermons and panegyrics. These include five sermons on the translation of the relics of John Chrysostom with a short Life of the saint, and encomia of Zechariah, Barbara, Joachim and Anna. Orations on the martyrs Samonas, Gurias and Abibus and on the Annunciation, along with hymns to the Theotokos, are also attributed to him.

Cynewulf was an Anglo-Saxon poet writing religious verse in Old English. He is one of the few Old English poets known by name, and his name survives because he worked it into his poems in runes. He probably flourished in the 9th century, though proposed dates run from the late 8th to the 10th. Four poems carry his runic signature: Elene, Juliana, The Fates of the Apostles and Christ II (The Ascension). Elene, Juliana and The Fates of the Apostles deal with saints and martyrs. Christ II is a homiletic poem drawing on Gregory the Great's homily on the Ascension. Cynewulf is regarded as a leading figure of Anglo-Saxon Christian poetry.

Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus (c. 200–210 to 258) was bishop of Carthage in Roman North Africa. He had a classical rhetorical education and was elected bishop in 249, soon after his conversion. He led his church through the Decian persecution and the dispute over readmitting the lapsed, opposed Novatian, and disagreed with Pope Stephen over baptism by heretics. He was martyred at Carthage under Valerian. His letters and treatises, including On the Unity of the Church, On the Lord's Prayer and On the Plague, made him the leading Latin Christian writer before Jerome and Augustine.

Cyprian of Toulon (Cyprianus Tolonensis, c. 476–546) was a Gallic churchman and bishop of Toulon in Provence in the first half of the sixth century. He was a disciple and close associate of Caesarius of Arles, took part in several southern Gallic councils of his day, and supported Caesarius's Augustinian teaching on grace. He is best known as the principal author of the first book of the Life of Caesarius of Arles, written soon after Caesarius's death in 542. A letter on a Christological question, addressed to Bishop Maximus of Geneva, also survives under his name.

Cyprianus Gallus, or Cyprian the Gaul (fl. c. 397–430), is the conventional name given to an anonymous Late Latin poet, probably from Gaul. He wrote an epic verse paraphrase of the historical books of the Old Testament, based on the Old Latin Bible. Only the part covering the first seven books, the Heptateuchos, survives. Its Genesis section once circulated under the name of Juvencus. The name was coined by the modern editor Rudolf Peiper, because the poem had wrongly been attributed to Cyprian of Carthage. The poems Carmen de Sodoma and Carmen de Iona are sometimes ascribed to him, though doubtfully.

Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444) was an Egyptian theologian who served as Patriarch of Alexandria from 412 until his death. He played a central part in the Christological controversies of the fifth century. He opposed Nestorius of Constantinople, defended the title Theotokos for the Virgin Mary, and presided over the Council of Ephesus in 431, which deposed Nestorius. His large body of writings includes biblical commentaries on the Pentateuch, the Minor Prophets and John, dogmatic treatises on the Incarnation and the Trinity, letters and festal homilies. He is venerated as a saint and Doctor of the Church.

Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 313–386) was a Greek theologian and bishop of Jerusalem from about 350. His hostile relations with Acacius of Caesarea and the policies of several emperors led to his exile more than once. He is best known for his Catechetical Lectures, a series of instructions given to candidates for baptism. They are introduced by the Procatechesis and followed by the Mystagogical Lectures on the sacraments, though some scholars attribute the latter to his successor John. These texts are important evidence for fourth-century catechesis and liturgy. He is venerated as a saint and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1883.

Cyril of Scythopolis (c. 525 – c. 559) was a Greek-speaking Christian monk, priest and hagiographer in sixth-century Palestine. He was born at Scythopolis (modern Beit She'an) and became a monk in the Judaean desert, living in the New Laura and later the Great Laura founded by Sabas. His Lives of the Palestinian monks include biographies of Euthymius, Sabas, John the Hesychast and others. They are a major source for the history of desert monasticism and for the Origenist controversies of his time. They are valued for their attention to chronology and topography.

Dagobert I (c. 603/605–639) was a Merovingian king of the Franks, son of Chlothar II. He ruled Austrasia from 623 and, from 629, Neustria and Burgundy as well, so that for a time he held all of Francia. He is often described as the last Merovingian king to hold real power before the mayors of the palace took control. Counselled by figures such as Eligius, he supported the church and became the first Frankish king buried at the Basilica of Saint-Denis. Ecclesiastical ordinances are attributed to him.

Dalmatius (died c. 440) was archimandrite of the monastery in Constantinople later named after him, and he held the title Archimandrite of the Monasteries, the city's chief monk. He was a former officer of the guard under Theodosius I. He left his family to become a monk under Isaac of Dalmatia. He fiercely opposed Nestorius. In 431 he left his monastery for the first time in decades and led a procession of monks to Theodosius II to support Cyril of Alexandria after the Council of Ephesus. A few letters and an apologia attributed to him survive. He is venerated as a saint on 3 August.

Daniel of Raithu (also Daniel of Raithou) was a Greek monk of Raithou, a monastic settlement on the Sinai peninsula. He probably lived in the first half of the seventh century. He is known only as the author of a short Life of John Climacus, the abbot of Mount Sinai and author of the Ladder of Divine Ascent. This brief biography is a main source for John's life and was often copied together with the Ladder. Little else is known about Daniel, and his exact dates are uncertain.

Diadochus of Photice was a fifth-century Greek ascetic writer and bishop of Photice in Epirus, active around the middle of the century. His dates are uncertain. His best-known work is the One Hundred Chapters on Spiritual Knowledge and Discernment. It teaches the prayer of the heart, the remembrance of God and discernment between grace and deception, and is partly directed against Messalian ideas. A sermon on the Ascension is also attributed to him. His writings are included in the Philokalia and influenced Maximus the Confessor, John Climacus and later Hesychasm. He is venerated as a saint on 29 March.

Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398) was a Christian theologian and teacher in Alexandria. He lost his sight in early childhood but became famous for his learning, and he taught in the city for about fifty years. Jerome and Rufinus were among his pupils. He followed Origen in his biblical interpretation and defended Nicene orthodoxy. His treatise On the Holy Spirit survives in Jerome's Latin translation. After Origenism was condemned in 553, his works stopped being copied and many were lost. Several of his commentaries were recovered among the Tura papyri found in 1941. Scholars disagree about whether he wrote De Trinitate.

Dinoot (Latin Dinothus) was abbot of the large British monastery of Bangor-is-y-Coed in northeast Wales in the early seventh century. Bede names him as abbot of Bangor at the time of the British bishops' meetings with Augustine of Canterbury, around 602–604.
