At those meetings the British clergy refused to accept Roman customs or Augustine's authority. A short reply to Augustine, the Responsio ad Augustinum, has been attributed to him and rejecting Roman jurisdiction. It is generally regarded as a much later forgery.

Dionysius Exiguus ("the Humble", c. 470 – c. 544) was a monk from Scythia Minor, one of the community of Scythian monks, who lived in Rome from about 500 until his death. He translated Greek theological and canonical texts into Latin, including the synodal letter of Cyril of Alexandria against Nestorius. His collections of conciliar canons and papal decretals, known as the Dionysiana, carried great authority in the Western Church. In 525 he drew up an Easter table for the years 532–626. In it he introduced the Anno Domini system of numbering years.

Dionysius of Alexandria, called "the Great", was bishop of Alexandria from 248 until his death in 264 or 265. A pupil of Origen, he led the catechetical school of Alexandria before becoming bishop. He lived through the persecutions of Decius and Valerian and was sent into exile. He took part in debates over the readmission of the lapsed, rebaptism, Sabellianism and millenarianism. He is also known for arguing on grounds of style that the Book of Revelation was not written by the author of the Fourth Gospel. His writings survive mostly as fragments of letters quoted by Eusebius. His Canonical Letter to Basilides is the one letter that survives complete.

Dionysius of Corinth was bishop of Corinth around AD 171 and is venerated as a saint. Eusebius of Caesarea calls him the author of "catholic epistles" to churches including Lacedaemon, Athens, Nicomedia, Gortyna and Knossos in Crete, Amastris, and Rome. His Ecclesiastical History summarises these letters and quotes from them. Only fragments survive, chiefly from his letter to Bishop Soter of Rome. It tells of the Roman church's generosity and of the letter of Clement being read in Corinth's assemblies. It also links Peter and Paul with both Corinth and Rome, and complains that his letters had been altered by others.

Dionysius the Areopagite was a first-century Athenian, a member or judge of the Areopagus court. The Acts of the Apostles (17:34) names him among those converted by the Apostle Paul's preaching in Athens. Later tradition, beginning with Dionysius of Corinth, made him the first bishop of Athens. Several Christian churches honour him as a saint and martyr. In the late fifth or early sixth century an anonymous author wrote influential theological works under his name, now known as the Pseudo-Dionysian corpus. Medieval Western tradition also wrongly identified him with Denis of Paris. No genuine writings by him survive.

Dorotheus of Gaza (c. 500 – after 560), also called Abba Dorotheus, was a Greek-speaking Christian monk and abbot of the sixth century. He trained at the monastery of Abba Seridus near Gaza under the elders Barsanuphius and John the Prophet. He later founded and led his own community. His Instructions (Doctrinae diversae) are practical talks on the ascetic life that stress humility, obedience, giving up one's own will and charity toward others. A few of his letters also survive. His teaching was widely read and shaped monastic formation in both East and West.

Blossius Aemilius Dracontius (c. 455 – c. 505) was a Christian Latin poet and lawyer from Carthage, in Roman Africa under Vandal rule. He came from a landowning family. After writing a poem praising a foreign ruler, he lost his property and was imprisoned by the Vandal king, usually identified as Gunthamund (484–496). From prison he wrote the Satisfactio, an elegiac plea for pardon. His main work is De laudibus Dei in three books, whose account of creation once circulated separately as the Hexameron. He also wrote secular mythological poems, the Carmina minora, and probably the Orestis Tragoedia.

Dynamius the Patrician (Dynamius Patricius) was a Gallo-Roman aristocrat and Latin writer of Provence, active in the late sixth century. He held high office as patrician or governor of Provence under the Frankish kings of Austrasia and corresponded with leading figures of his day, including Venantius Fortunatus and Pope Gregory the Great. He wrote a Life of Maximus, the fifth-century abbot of Lérins and bishop of Riez, which was later adapted into a Life of Virgilius of Arles. He also wrote a Life of the abbot Marius. Two of his letters also survive.

Egeria, also called Etheria or Aetheria, was a Christian woman, probably from Gallaecia in Hispania or from Gaul. She is widely regarded as the author of the earliest surviving detailed account of a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, made about 381–384. Her long letter in Latin, known as the Itinerarium Egeriae or Peregrinatio Aetheriae, was addressed to a circle of women at home. It describes holy sites in Sinai, Palestine, Egypt and Mesopotamia and the liturgy of Jerusalem. The text was once ascribed to Silvia of Aquitaine. It survives incomplete and is also valuable evidence for late spoken Latin.

Eleutherius of Tournai (died c. 531/532) is venerated as a saint and is traditionally regarded as the first bishop of Tournai in northern Gaul. Very little is known about him historically. He was probably made bishop after Remigius of Reims organised the church in the region at the end of the fifth century. According to tradition he was a lifelong friend of Medardus, and both men served at court before becoming bishops. Several Latin sermons on the Trinity, the Nativity and the Annunciation carry his name, but they are spurious.

Elpis is a shadowy figure of the early sixth century in the Latin tradition. Later tradition calls her the wife of the Roman philosopher and statesman Boethius, but she is named only in pseudonymous or late sources. Boethius's wife is otherwise known as Rusticiana, daughter of Symmachus, so this identification is doubtful. Medieval tradition credited Elpis with Latin hymns for the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, among them "Aurea luce et decore roseo". These attributions, and her very existence as a historical person, remain uncertain.

Severus Sanctus Endelechius (or Endelechus) was a Latin Christian poet and rhetorician of the late fourth century. He is often identified with the rhetor Severus who was a friend of Paulinus of Nola. He wrote a short bucolic poem known as De mortibus boum ("On the Deaths of Cattle"), also titled Carmen bucolicum de virtute signi crucis Domini. In it, herdsmen talk about a cattle plague, which modern scholars have identified as rinderpest. One herdsman's cattle are spared through the sign of the cross. The poem joins the classical pastoral tradition with Christian apologetics.

Magnus Felix Ennodius (473 or 474–521) was a Latin rhetorician, poet and bishop of Pavia (Ticinum) from about 514. He came from a Gallo-Roman aristocratic family, probably born at Arles, and spent much of his career as a cleric in Milan. He strongly supported Pope Symmachus in the Laurentian schism, defending the synod that acquitted him, and later served Pope Hormisdas on embassies to Constantinople. His works include letters, poems, rhetorical declamations (dictiones), a panegyric of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric and a Life of Epiphanius of Pavia. He is venerated as a saint, with a feast on 17 July.

Ephraim of Cherson (Ephraem Chersonensis) was a bishop of Cherson in the Crimea who wrote in Greek. Almost nothing is known of his life, and his dates are uncertain; he is usually placed somewhere between the sixth and ninth centuries. He is known for an account of a miracle of Clement of Rome, whose tomb tradition placed in the sea near Cherson. The account tells how a child was preserved at the tomb, which the sea uncovered each year. He should not be confused with Ephraim, one of the fourth-century martyred bishops of Cherson.

Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373) was a Syriac Christian theologian, deacon and poet. He was born in Nisibis and moved to Edessa after the city was handed over to Persia in 363. He is regarded as the greatest hymnographer of Syriac literature. His teaching hymns (madrāšê), including the Hymns on the Nativity and the Nisibene Hymns, were sung by women's choirs. He also wrote verse homilies, biblical commentaries and prose refutations of Mani, Marcion and Bardaisan. Many works were later falsely attributed to him. In 1920 the Catholic Church declared him a Doctor of the Church.

Epiphanius (died 5 June 535) was Patriarch of Constantinople from 25 February 520 until his death, succeeding John of Cappadocia. He held office under the emperors Justin I and Justinian I, soon after the healing of the Acacian schism between Constantinople and Rome. He supported the Chalcedonian settlement and corresponded with Pope Hormisdas on church unity and the reception of bishops. His surviving writings are mostly letters and synodal statements. He was succeeded by Anthimus I.

Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–320 – 403) was born in Palestine and founded a monastery near Eleutheropolis. In 367 he became bishop of Salamis (Constantia) on Cyprus. He was a vigorous defender of Nicene orthodoxy and a fierce opponent of Origenism, which drew him into disputes with John of Jerusalem and John Chrysostom. His Ancoratus sets out the doctrine of the Trinity. His best-known work, the Panarion, is a catalogue and refutation of eighty heresies that also covers pagan and philosophical schools. It preserves much otherwise lost information on early sects. He also opposed some uses of religious images.

Epiphanius the Monk (Epiphanius Monachus) was a Byzantine monk and priest of the Kallistratos monastery in Constantinople. He lived in the 8th or 9th century, though his exact dates are uncertain. He wrote a Life of the Virgin Mary, one of the earliest Greek biographies of her, and a Life of the Apostle Andrew, which gathers traditions about the apostle's missionary journeys. He is also credited with the first Greek guidebook to Jerusalem and the Holy Land for pilgrims, which was later translated into Old Church Slavonic.

Eraclius (or Heraclius) was a presbyter of Hippo Regius in Roman North Africa in the early fifth century. In 426 Augustine publicly named him as his successor before the clergy and people of Hippo, and the proceedings are recorded in Augustine's Letter 213. Augustine stayed bishop but handed much of the church's administrative and judicial business over to him. Eraclius also paid for a shrine to the martyr Stephen at Hippo. One sermon of his survives, preached while Augustine was present. Nothing certain is known of his later career.

Erechthius was a Greek bishop of Antioch in Pisidia in Asia Minor. He served sometime between the Council of Ephesus (431) and 448, probably around 440. His Christology was Miaphysite. Two sermons are attributed to him. One, on the Epiphany, was preached in Constantinople before Patriarch Proclus. It survives as excerpts in florilegia and defends the title Theotokos and Mary's virginity in giving birth. The other, on the Nativity, survives only in Syriac. Timothy Aelurus cited him against the Council of Chalcedon, while Chalcedonian writers such as Ephraim of Antioch tried to refute him.

Æthelberht (born mid-sixth century, died 616) was King of Kent from about 589 and the first Anglo-Saxon king to become a Christian. Bede counts him among the kings who held overlordship over other English kingdoms. Through his marriage to the Frankish Christian princess Bertha, he welcomed Augustine's mission from Pope Gregory I in 597, accepted baptism soon after and gave the missionaries land in Canterbury. His law code is the earliest surviving written law in any Germanic language. Latin charters granting land to churches carry his name, but their authenticity is widely doubted. He is venerated as a saint.

Eucherius of Lyon (c. 380 – c. 449) was a Gallo-Roman aristocrat, monk and bishop. With his wife Galla he withdrew to the monastic community of the Lérins islands, where his sons Salonius and Veranus were educated; both later became bishops. Around 434–439 he became bishop of Lyon. He wrote De laude eremi, in praise of the desert life, addressed to Hilary of Arles, and a letter on contempt for the world. He also wrote two exegetical handbooks, the Formulae spiritalis intellegentiae and the Instructiones. An account of the martyrdom of the Theban Legion at Agaunum is attributed to him. He is venerated as a saint.

Aelia Eudocia (c. 400–460) was an Eastern Roman empress, the wife of Emperor Theodosius II. She was born Athenais, the daughter of an Athenian philosopher, and took the name Eudocia when she was baptised and married in 421. She was a learned Greek poet. Her works include the Homerocentones, which retell biblical stories in lines taken from Homer, and a hexameter poem on the legend of Saint Cyprian of Antioch. After falling out with her husband, she settled permanently in Jerusalem. There she supported the local population and built churches, and she died there. She is venerated as a saint.

Eugenius of Ancyra was a fourth-century Greek churchman, a deacon of the Christian community at Ancyra (modern Ankara) that remained loyal to the controversial bishop Marcellus of Ancyra. Around 371–372 he travelled to Alexandria and gave Athanasius a profession of faith, the Expositio fidei ad Athanasium. It aimed to show that the Marcellians held orthodox Nicene views of the Trinity and to win them communion with Athanasius and the Egyptian bishops. The document is an important witness to the later history of the Marcellian party during the Trinitarian controversies. Little else is known of his life.

Eugenius of Carthage (died 505) was a Latin bishop and saint. In 480 he was unanimously elected Bishop of Carthage to succeed Deogratias, during the rule of the Arian Vandal kings over North Africa. He led the Catholic, Nicene party against Arianism. For the conference that King Huneric called in 484 he presented a profession of faith on behalf of the Catholic bishops of Africa. He was exiled, and he wrote a letter urging the people of Carthage to hold to the Catholic faith. He was later recalled but exiled again, and died in exile in Gaul, near Albi.

Eugippius (c. 460 – c. 535) was a Latin monastic writer and abbot. As a disciple of Severinus of Noricum, he lived through the last years of Roman rule on the Danube frontier. After the Roman population left Noricum, he settled with Severinus's community at Castellum Lucullanum near Naples and later became its abbot. He is best known for his Life of Saint Severinus (c. 511), a key source for the end of Roman rule in the Danube provinces. He also compiled a widely copied anthology of excerpts from Augustine, dedicated to the virgin Proba, and is credited with a monastic rule.

Eulogius of Alexandria (died 607 or 608) was the Greek, Chalcedonian Patriarch of Alexandria from about 580 until his death. Before becoming patriarch he was a priest and monastic superior at Antioch. He defended the Council of Chalcedon against Miaphysite opponents such as the Severians, and also wrote against the Novatians and the Agnoetae. He was a friend and correspondent of Pope Gregory the Great, and several of Gregory's letters to him survive. Most of his own writings are lost. They are known mainly from summaries in Photius's Bibliotheca and from surviving sermons and fragments. He is venerated as a saint, with a feast day on 13 June.

Eumenius was a Gallo-Roman rhetorician and one of the Latin panegyrists of the late third and early fourth centuries. He taught rhetoric at Augustodunum (Autun) and served as magister memoriae under Constantius Chlorus. His one securely attributed speech is Panegyrici Latini IX, delivered at Autun around 298, which pleads for the restoration of the city's schools. Earlier scholars credited him with other anonymous speeches in the collection, including the orations to Constantine of 310 and 311. Modern scholarship generally rejects these attributions.

Eunomius of Cyzicus (died c. 393) was a Greek theologian and a leader of the Anomoeans. This was the most extreme wing of fourth-century Arianism, and its followers were often called Eunomians. He was born in Cappadocia or Pontus and studied under Aetius at Alexandria. Eudoxius of Antioch ordained him deacon, and in 360 he became bishop of Cyzicus, but he was deposed within a year. He taught that the Son is unlike the Father in essence. His Liber apologeticus (Apology) provoked refutations from Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nyssa. He was exiled several times.

Euphronius of Autun was a Gallo-Roman bishop of Autun in the second half of the fifth century, venerated as a saint. His episcopate is usually placed from about 450, and he was still alive after 472. Sidonius Apollinaris admired him, and Gregory of Tours records that he built a church over the tomb of Saint Symphorian. With Lupus of Troyes he took part in choosing a bishop for Chalon-sur-Saône around 470. The two bishops also wrote a surviving letter to Thalassius of Angers that answers questions of church discipline and clerical marriage.

Eusebius of Alexandria is the name attached to a collection of Greek homilies of uncertain date, usually placed between the fifth and seventh centuries. About twenty-two homilies survive under his name. The collection comes with a legendary life of Eusebius credited to a John the Notary, who may be the real author, so Eusebius himself is often taken to be a fictional figure. The homilies deal with moral and liturgical subjects, among them the observance of Sunday (De die dominica). They spread widely and were translated into Latin and several Eastern languages.

Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260/265–339/340), also called Eusebius Pamphili, was a Greek Christian scholar, historian and exegete. He was a student and collaborator of Pamphilus, and around 314 he became bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. He is known as the "Father of Church History" for his Ecclesiastical History. His other writings include the Chronicle, the Preparation for the Gospel and Demonstration of the Gospel, the Theophania, the Onomasticon, commentaries on the Psalms and Isaiah, and the Life of Constantine. He took part in the Council of Nicaea in 325.

Eusebius of Emesa (c. 300 – c. 359/360) was a Greek-speaking bishop and theologian, born at Edessa and educated at Caesarea, Antioch and Alexandria, where his teachers included Eusebius of Caesarea. In 339 he declined the see of Alexandria and then became bishop of Emesa (Homs). His skill in astronomy led his congregation to accuse him of sorcery, but it won him favour with Emperor Constantius II. He leaned towards the semi-Arian party. Jerome praised his eloquence, and he was known for literal biblical exegesis in the Antiochene manner. Of his many writings, only fragments and some homilies survive, most of them in translation.

Eusebius of Vercelli (died 371) was a Sardinian-born churchman. He became the first bishop of Vercelli in northern Italy around 345. His birth date, traditionally given as about 283, is uncertain. He was a firm defender of Nicene orthodoxy and Athanasius against Arianism. At the Council of Milan in 355 he refused to condemn Athanasius and was exiled to Scythopolis, Cappadocia and the Thebaid. He took part in the Council of Alexandria in 362 and later returned to the West. He is remembered for having his clergy live a shared, monastic-style life. A few of his letters survive.

Eustathius, called Afer ("the African"), was a Latin translator active in the early fifth century. Almost nothing is known of his life beyond his name, which suggests a North African origin. He is remembered for his Latin version of Basil of Caesarea's Hexaemeron, the nine Greek homilies on the six days of creation. His translation made Basil's exegesis of Genesis available to Latin readers in the West, and Cassiodorus later mentioned it as a useful work.

Eustathius of Antioch, sometimes called "the Great", was a fourth-century Greek bishop. A native of Side in Pamphylia, he was first bishop of Beroea and then became bishop of Antioch around 324. He was a strong opponent of Arianism at the Council of Nicaea in 325. Around 330 he was deposed by his opponents and exiled to Thrace, and the date of his death is uncertain. His loyal followers in Antioch kept up a separate community for decades. His main surviving work, De engastrimytho, deals with the witch of Endor and attacks Origen's allegorical exegesis. Other writings survive only in fragments.

Eustathius of Berytus was bishop of Berytus (modern Beirut) in Phoenicia in the mid-fifth century, during the Christological controversies. At the Second Council of Ephesus in 449 he supported Dioscorus of Alexandria. At the Council of Chalcedon in 451 he changed sides and accepted the council's settlement. He is also known for his dispute with Photius of Tyre over metropolitan rights in Phoenicia, after Theodosius II raised Berytus to the rank of a metropolis. Only fragments of his writings on Christ's natures survive.

Eustathius the Monk (Eustathius Monachus) was a Greek Chalcedonian writer of the sixth century, active around the middle of the century. Almost nothing is known of his life. He is remembered for a letter to Timothy, a scholasticus, on the two natures of Christ. In it he defends the Chalcedonian teaching that Christ is one person in two natures. He argues against the Christology of Severus of Antioch, the leading Miaphysite theologian, and quotes Severus's writings to show that they contradict themselves. The letter is an example of the Christological controversy that followed the Council of Chalcedon.

Euthalius the Deacon was a Greek Christian scholar remembered as the author of the "Euthalian Apparatus." This set of editorial aids accompanies the Acts of the Apostles, the Catholic Epistles and the Pauline Epistles. It includes prologues, summaries of chapters, lists of Old Testament quotations, and a layout of the text in sense-lines. Later tradition calls him a deacon of Alexandria and afterwards bishop of Sulca, a see that cannot be securely located, with a death date of 459. His identity and dates are disputed, and modern estimates range from the fourth to the seventh century. His apparatus strongly shaped the presentation of New Testament manuscripts.

Eutherius of Tyana was metropolitan bishop of Tyana in Cappadocia in the early fifth century. At the Council of Ephesus in 431 he belonged to the eastern party led by John of Antioch and supported Nestorius against Cyril of Alexandria. He opposed the reconciliation of 433, was deposed and exiled to Scythopolis, and later found refuge with Irenaeus of Tyre. His polemical treatise known as the Protest (Antilogia) defends Antiochene Christology. It was long transmitted under the name of Athanasius, and Photius attributed it to Theodoret. Excerpts of his writings also survive in Latin translation by Marius Mercator.

Euthymius the Athonite (c. 955–1028), also called Euthymius the Iberian (Ekvtime Mtatsmindeli in Georgian), was a Georgian monk, scholar and saint from Tao-Klarjeti. He was the son of John the Iberian, who taught him Greek and Georgian. Euthymius helped found the Iviron monastery on Mount Athos and later became its abbot. He was one of the most productive translators of Greek patristic, liturgical and biblical texts into Georgian, including the Book of Revelation. He is also widely credited with the Greek version of the Barlaam and Ioasaph legend, which was adapted from a Georgian original, though that attribution is debated.

Eutropius of Valencia (died c. 610) was a Hispano-Roman monk and bishop in Visigothic Spain. He was abbot of the Servitanum monastery and a leading figure at the Third Council of Toledo in 589. Soon afterwards he became Bishop of Valencia, and he is thought to have died no earlier than 610. Little is known of his time as bishop. Two Latin letters to a bishop named Peter survive under his name. One deals with discipline and correction in monastic communities, and the other with the eight principal vices. Later writers often called him a saint, but there is no evidence of a liturgical cult.

Eutychius (c. 512–582) was Patriarch of Constantinople from 552 to 565 and again from 577 to 582. He is venerated as a saint in the Orthodox and Catholic churches. Appointed under Justinian I, he presided over the Second Council of Constantinople in 553 during the Three Chapters controversy. In 565 he was deposed and exiled after opposing the emperor's support for aphthartodocetism. After his return, his teaching that the risen body would be intangible was disputed by the future Pope Gregory the Great. His surviving writings include a discourse on Easter and the Eucharist and a letter to Pope Vigilius.

Evagrius Gallus, also called Evagrius Monachus, was a Latin Christian writer from Gaul who was active in the first half of the fifth century. Very little is known about his life. Gennadius of Marseille names him as the author of the Altercatio legis inter Simonem Iudaeum et Theophilum Christianum, an anti-Jewish apologetic dialogue. In it the Christian Theophilus argues from Old Testament proof-texts that Jesus is the Messiah, and the Jew Simon is finally convinced and asks for baptism. The work draws on earlier Latin writers such as Tertullian and Cyprian.

Evagrius Ponticus (345–399), also called Evagrius the Solitary, was a Christian monk, ascetic and theologian from Pontus. He studied under Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus and served in the church at Constantinople. He then left for Jerusalem, where in 383 he became a monk under Rufinus and Melania the Elder. He spent his last years among the desert monks of Nitria and Kellia in Egypt. His works include the Praktikos, the Chapters on Prayer and the Kephalaia Gnostica. His scheme of eight evil thoughts shaped later teaching on the deadly sins. He influenced John Cassian and later monasticism, even though some of his Origenist ideas were condemned.

Evagrius Scholasticus (c. 536–c. 594) was a Greek-writing church historian born at Epiphania in Syria. He trained as a lawyer, which is where the title "Scholasticus" comes from, and worked in Antioch as an aide and legal adviser to Patriarch Gregory of Antioch. His Ecclesiastical History, in six books, continues the work of earlier church historians. It covers events from the First Council of Ephesus (431) to the reign of Emperor Maurice. Written from a Chalcedonian standpoint, it is an important source for the Christological controversies of the period and for the Justinianic plague, which he survived as a child.

Evodius (died c. 424–426) was a North African bishop and a close friend of Augustine of Hippo. Like Augustine, he came from Thagaste. He served as an imperial official before converting, joined Augustine's circle in Italy and was present at the death of Augustine's mother, Monica, at Ostia. He is a speaker in Augustine's dialogues On the Greatness of the Soul and On Free Will. From about 396 he was bishop of Uzalis, and letters he exchanged with Augustine about the soul survive. He brought relics of Saint Stephen to Uzalis. The anti-Manichaean treatise De fide contra Manichaeos is attributed to him.

Facundus of Hermiane was a sixth-century Latin theologian and bishop of Hermiana, a town in the Roman province of Byzacena in North Africa. Little is known of his life beyond his part in the Three Chapters controversy. He was in Constantinople when Emperor Justinian condemned writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrus and Ibas of Edessa. Facundus held that this condemnation undermined the Council of Chalcedon, and he defended the Three Chapters in his twelve books Pro defensione trium capitulorum. He later had to go into hiding. Together with other African bishops he broke communion with Pope Vigilius, and he continued the dispute in his work Contra Mocianum.

Fastidius was a British bishop of the early fifth century. He is known mainly from Gennadius of Marseille, who describes him as a bishop of the Britons and credits him with a treatise On the Christian Life, addressed to a certain Fatalis, and a work on keeping widowhood. The surviving De vita Christiana, handed down among the works of Augustine, is often attributed to him. Its moral teaching links it to the Pelagian movement, and some scholars connect him with other anonymous Pelagian writings. Little else about his life is known for certain.

Faustinus was a Latin Christian homilist who probably lived in the late fifth century, perhaps around 480–500, though his exact dates are uncertain. Almost nothing is known of his life, office or location. A sermon on the Passion of the Lord (Homilia de passione Domini) is attributed to him. He should not be confused with Faustinus, the Luciferian presbyter of the fourth century.

Faustinus was a Latin presbyter of the later fourth century and a leading member of the Luciferians. This rigorist faction, named after Lucifer of Cagliari, refused communion with Arians and with Arian converts to Nicene Christology. In 383 or 384 he and the presbyter Marcellinus travelled to Constantinople and presented the Libellus precum to Emperor Theodosius I. It is an important statement of Luciferian views, and Theodosius answered it with a rescript granting the group protection. Faustinus also wrote a Confessio fidei addressed to Theodosius and a treatise against the Arians, De Trinitate, addressed to the Empress Flaccilla.

Faustus of Riez (c. 405/410–c. 490/495) was a Gallic monk and bishop, probably of British origin. He became a monk and then abbot of Lérins, and from about 460 he was bishop of Riez in Provence. Around 477 the Visigothic king Euric sent him into exile, and he later returned to his see. He rejected Pelagianism but also opposed strict predestinarianism. In De gratia he argued that human free will cooperates with grace, a position later called "Semi-Pelagian" and opposed at the Council of Orange (529). He also wrote on the Holy Spirit, along with letters and sermons.

Fulgentius Ferrandus (died 546/547) was a Latin theologian and deacon of the church of Carthage in Roman North Africa. He was a pupil of Fulgentius of Ruspe, and the Life of Fulgentius is usually attributed to him. His surviving letters answer questions on doctrine and church practice, among them a letter to Eugippius on the Trinity. In the Three Chapters controversy he opposed Justinian's condemnation of the three writers. His Breviatio canonum, a summary of conciliar canons arranged by subject, was an important early collection of church law.

Ferreolus (Ferréol) of Uzès (d. 581) was a Gallo-Roman bishop in Merovingian Gaul. He was born in the early sixth century, possibly at Narbonne, and was bishop of Uzès from about 553 until his death. He founded a monastery and wrote a Latin rule for it, the Regula ad monachos, which survives. The rule is noted for treating the copying of manuscripts as equal to manual labour. According to his Vita, Childebert I banished him around 555 for being too friendly with the local Jews. After returning, he preached to them to convert them and expelled those who refused baptism. His feast is 4 January.

Filastrius (Philastrius or Philaster) was a Latin bishop of Brescia in northern Italy in the late fourth century. He died around 397 and is venerated as a saint. Before becoming bishop he travelled widely preaching against Arianism, and he attended the Council of Aquileia in 381. He is known for the Diversarum hereseon liber, a catalogue of 156 heresies. It covers errors from before Christ as well as Christian ones, and Augustine and later heresiologists drew on it. His successor Gaudentius wrote a sermon in his honour, which is the main account of his life.

Furius Dionysius Filocalus was a Roman calligrapher, scribe and stone engraver who worked in the second half of the fourth century. In 354 he produced the illustrated Chronograph of 354 for a wealthy Roman Christian named Valentinus. This collection of calendrical and chronological texts includes the earliest known reference to Christmas being celebrated on 25 December. Filocalus later designed the elegant lettering used for the verse inscriptions that Pope Damasus I set up in the Roman catacombs to honour the martyrs. This distinctive style is known as Filocalian or Damasine script.

Julius Firmicus Maternus was a fourth-century Latin writer of senatorial rank, apparently from Sicily, who lived under Constantine I and his sons. He worked as an advocate and then as an astrologer. Around 334–337 he wrote the Matheseos libri octo, the most extensive Roman astrological handbook to survive. After converting to Christianity, he composed De errore profanarum religionum around 346 and dedicated it to the emperors Constantius II and Constans. In this apologetic work he attacks the pagan mystery cults and the worship of the elements, and he urges the emperors to suppress paganism by force.

Firmilian (died c. 268–269) was bishop of Caesarea Mazaca in Cappadocia from about 232. He was a disciple and friend of Origen and one of the most respected eastern bishops of his time. In the mid-third-century controversy over baptism by heretics, he sided with Cyprian of Carthage in requiring that such converts be rebaptised, and Pope Stephen I excommunicated him for it. His only surviving work is a letter to Cyprian, written about 256 and preserved in Latin among Cyprian's correspondence. It refers to the Council of Iconium's ruling against the baptism of the Cataphrygians, or Montanists. He later took part in the synods held at Antioch against Paul of Samosata.

Firmus was bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia in the first half of the fifth century and died around 439. He took part in the Council of Ephesus in 431, where he firmly supported Cyril of Alexandria against Nestorius. He was active in the Christological controversy that followed the council. Firmus is known mainly for a collection of Greek letters to clergy, officials and friends, written in a careful rhetorical style. Other short writings connected with the Ephesine dispute are also attributed to him.

Flavian (died 449) was archbishop of Constantinople from 446 to 449. In 448 a synod he presided over in Constantinople condemned the archimandrite Eutyches for teaching that Christ had only one nature after the union. Flavian reported the case to Pope Leo I, whose reply, known as Leo's Tome, set out the doctrine of Christ's two natures. At the Second Council of Ephesus in 449, the so-called Robber Synod, Flavian was deposed. Tradition holds that he was beaten there and died shortly afterwards. The Council of Chalcedon (451) vindicated him, and he is venerated as a saint and martyr.

Florentius was a Latin correspondent of Lucifer, the anti-Arian bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia, and was active around 360. He is generally identified as an official at the court of the emperor Constantius II, possibly the magister officiorum. A short letter from him to Lucifer survives with Lucifer's writings. In it he acknowledges that the bishop's polemical books, written against the emperor's religious policy, had been received at court. Little else is known about his life.

Florianus was a sixth-century Latin abbot of the monastery of Romainmôtier, in what is now the canton of Vaud in Switzerland. The monastery took its name from Romanus of Condat, who founded it. Florianus is known almost entirely from a letter to Nicetius, bishop of Trier, written around the 550s. In it he addresses the bishop with great respect and asks for his friendship and prayers. The letter survives in the Epistolae Austrasicae, a Merovingian collection of letters. It gives a rare look at contacts between Jura monasteries and Frankish bishops. Little else is known of his life.

Florus of Lyon (Florus Lugdunensis) was a deacon of the church of Lyon. He was active in the first half of the ninth century and died around 860. He was a theologian, canonist, liturgist and poet, and he ran the scriptorium at Lyon. He was counted among the leading theological authorities of the Frankish clergy. He opposed Amalarius of Metz on the liturgy and wrote against John Scotus Eriugena during the predestination controversy. He compiled patristic commentaries on the Pauline epistles, chiefly from Augustine. An expanded version of Bede's martyrology is attributed to him, and he also wrote Latin poems.

Fredegar, or Fredegarius, is the conventional name given to the unknown author or authors of a seventh-century Frankish chronicle in Latin. The chronicle was probably written in Burgundy, and the name was first attached to it only in the sixteenth century. It runs from the creation of the world to 642, with a few references to events up to about 658. Later Carolingian continuations carry the story on to 768. The work is a key source for Merovingian history after 591, where Gregory of Tours' history ends. It also preserves the earliest account of Samo's Slavic realm.

Fabius Claudius Gordianus Fulgentius (462 or 467 – 527 or 533) was a North African theologian and bishop of Ruspe in Byzacena, in present-day Tunisia. He came from a noble family and worked as a civil official before becoming a monk. Under the Arian Vandal kings he was exiled to Sardinia for his Nicene faith. He was a leading follower of Augustine on grace and predestination and wrote against Arianism and Pelagianism. His works include Ad Monimum, Contra Arianos and De fide ad Petrum, which was long copied among Augustine's writings. He is venerated as a saint.

Gaudentius (died c. 410) was bishop of Brescia in northern Italy from about 387, succeeding Philastrius. He was chosen bishop while travelling in the East and was consecrated by Ambrose of Milan. In 404–405 he took part in a Western embassy to Constantinople in support of John Chrysostom, who later wrote to thank him. His surviving works are a collection of Latin sermons, or tractatus. They include a series of Easter-week addresses to the newly baptized, which he wrote down at the request of a man named Benivolus, and a sermon on Philastrius, his predecessor.

Gennadius I was patriarch of Constantinople from August 458 until his death on 17 November 471. He was a learned writer and followed the literal approach to biblical interpretation of the School of Antioch. Little of his work survives intact. Fragments of his scriptural commentaries, especially on Genesis and the Pauline epistles, survive in catenae. Early in his career he wrote a critique of Cyril of Alexandria's anathematisms. As patriarch, he issued an encyclical letter against simony, the buying and selling of ordination. The Eastern Orthodox Church commemorates him on 17 November.

Gennadius of Marseilles (died c. 496), also called Gennadius Massiliensis or Scholasticus, was a priest, monk and historian at Marseilles in southern Gaul. His best-known work is De viris illustribus, a continuation of Jerome's book of the same name. It gives short notices of about ninety Christian writers, many from the fifth century, and is a key source for the literary history of the period. He also wrote De ecclesiasticis dogmatibus, a summary of Christian doctrine that was long passed down among the works of Augustine. His theology has often been linked to the so-called Semi-Pelagian views held by some in Gaul.

George of Nicomedia was a Byzantine churchman and preacher of the ninth century. He served at Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, where he was chartophylax. He later became metropolitan of Nicomedia, probably under Patriarch Photius, who was his friend and correspondent. George is best known for his homilies, or orationes, many of them on the Virgin Mary. They treat her conception, birth and presentation in the Temple, and her presence at the Cross and the Passion. He also wrote liturgical hymns. His sermons are an important witness to Marian devotion in middle Byzantine preaching.

George of Pisidia (Georgios Pisides) was a Byzantine poet from Pisidia in Asia Minor, active in Constantinople during the reign of Emperor Heraclius (610–641). He was a deacon and cleric of Hagia Sophia and was closely linked to Patriarch Sergius. He wrote mainly in iambic twelve-syllable verse. His historical poems praise Heraclius' campaigns: the Persian Expedition, the Avar War, which describes the siege of Constantinople in 626, and the Heraclias. He also wrote theological and moral poems, among them the Hexaemeron, On the Vanity of Life and Against Severus. He did much to shape the main features of later Byzantine poetry.

George the Athonite, or Hagiorite (1009–1065), was a Georgian monk, theologian, calligrapher and translator. He served as hegumen of the Iviron Monastery on Mount Athos and led Georgian monastic communities in the Byzantine Empire. From Greek he translated Church Fathers, exegetical works and synaxaria. He also revised the Georgian Gospels, Psalter and liturgical books, including the translations of his predecessor Euthymius. His main original work is the Lives of John and Euthymius. In Georgia he helped regulate canon law and defended the autocephaly of the Georgian Church against Antioch. He is venerated as a saint.

George the Monk was a Byzantine monk in Constantinople in the reign of Michael III (842–867). He is often called Hamartolos, "the sinner", after the humble epithet he used for himself in his work's title. Everything known about him comes from his chronicle, which runs from the Creation to the death of the emperor Theophilus in 842. It has a strongly monastic, anti-iconoclast outlook, and its history is mixed with moral and theological reflection. Later writers continued it to 948. The chronicle was widely read and was translated into Old Slavonic and Georgian.

Germanus I (c. 634–740) was a Byzantine churchman who served as patriarch of Constantinople from 715 to 730, after earlier being bishop of Cyzicus. He opposed the iconoclast policy of Emperor Leo III, who forced him to resign in 730. He is venerated as a saint in both the Orthodox and Catholic Churches, with a feast day on 12 May. His works include homilies on the Virgin Mary, especially on her Presentation and Dormition, a treatise on heresies and councils, and letters defending the veneration of icons. He is also credited with the Historia ecclesiastica et mystica contemplatio, an influential commentary on the Byzantine liturgy.

Germanus (Germain) of Paris (c. 496–576) was a Gallic churchman, born near Autun, who served as abbot of Saint-Symphorien at Autun before becoming bishop of Paris around 555. He had close ties to the Merovingian court, and with King Childebert I he founded the abbey later known as Saint-Germain-des-Prés. A surviving letter to Queen Brunhild urges her to prevent civil war between the Frankish kings. An exposition of the Gallican liturgy is traditionally attributed to him, though the attribution is disputed. Venantius Fortunatus wrote his Life, and he is venerated as a saint, remembered as a friend of the poor.

Gildas, called Gildas Sapiens ("the Wise"), was a British monk of the sixth century. He was born around 450–500 and died around 570. He is best known for De Excidio et Conquestu Britanniae (On the Ruin and Conquest of Britain), a Latin polemic. It recounts the history of the Britons before and during the Saxon invasions and fiercely rebukes the kings and clergy of his day for their sins. His work is one of the few sources written in Britain during the sub-Roman period, and he was admired for his knowledge of the Bible and his learned style. Late in life he is said to have gone to Brittany and founded the monastery of Saint-Gildas-de-Rhuys.

Giorgi Merchule was a tenth-century Georgian monk, calligrapher and writer at the monastery of Khandzta in Tao, a region now in northeastern Turkey. His epithet "Merchule" is not a surname. It is usually taken to mean "specialist in canon law" or "theologian." In 951 he wrote the Life of Gregory of Khandzta, about the monastic founder Grigol Khandzteli (759–861). The work shows a wide knowledge of canon law and patristic literature and takes an unusual interest in the world around its subject. It is counted among the masterpieces of Old Georgian hagiographic prose.

Gregentius (Gregentios) was the supposed archbishop of Ẓafār (Taphar), capital of the South Arabian kingdom of Ḥimyar, in the mid-6th century. He is known almost entirely from a Greek hagiographical dossier compiled in the 10th century, which also survives in Slavonic. The dossier is largely legendary, though parts of it have some historical value. It has three parts: a Life of the saint, a law code he supposedly drew up for the Ḥimyarites (the Nomoi or Leges Homeritarum), and a long debate with a Jew named Herban (the Dialexis).

Gregory of Agrigentum (c. 559–c. 630) was a Sicilian bishop of Agrigento from 590 until at least 603. He wrote letters to Pope Gregory I. He is probably the subject of two semi-legendary saints' lives, one of them a Greek life attributed to Leontius. He is also traditionally named as the author of a Greek commentary on Ecclesiastes, the Explanatio in Ecclesiasten, which reads the book in both its literal and its spiritual sense. Scholars have questioned both identifications. He is commemorated as a saint, with a feast on 23 November in the Eastern Orthodox calendar.

Gregory of Antioch (died 593) was the Chalcedonian Patriarch of Antioch from about 570 until his death. He first became a monk in Jerusalem and later served as abbot on Sinai. Emperor Justin II made him patriarch after deposing Anastasius I. His aide Evagrius Scholasticus wrote about his career, which included accusations of paganism and a trial in Constantinople that ended in his acquittal. During Emperor Maurice's reign he calmed a mutiny of Roman troops in the war with Persia. His surviving Greek works include two sermons on Christ's baptism, a homily on the myrrh-bearing women and an address to the army.

Gregory of Dekapolis (Gregory Dekapolites), born before 797, was a ninth-century Byzantine monk and saint from the Isaurian Decapolis in Asia Minor. He travelled widely across the Byzantine world as a wandering ascetic and became known as "the New Miracle-Worker" for the wonders credited to him. He lived through the second period of Byzantine Iconoclasm and died in Constantinople in 842 or perhaps earlier. Ignatius the Deacon wrote his Life. A small number of short writings, including a sermon telling an edifying story, have come down under his name. His feast is kept on 20 November.

Gregory of Elvira (Gregorius Illiberitanus, died c. 392) was bishop of Elvira (Illiberis, near modern Granada) in the Roman province of Baetica, Spain. He was a firm defender of the Nicene faith against Arianism and sympathised with the rigorist stance of Lucifer of Cagliari. Jerome mentions him as still living in the early 390s. His treatise De fide orthodoxa contra Arianos was long transmitted under the names of Ambrose and Phoebadius of Agen. He also wrote exegetical works, including the Tractatus Origenis, a set of homilies on Scripture, and homilies on the Song of Songs.

Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390), also called Gregory the Theologian, was a Greek theologian, orator and poet from Cappadocia. He was one of the Cappadocian Fathers, together with Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nyssa. He served briefly as archbishop of Constantinople (380–381) and presided for a time over the Council of 381 before resigning. His five Theological Orations, which defend the divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit against the Eunomians, shaped Trinitarian doctrine. He also left many other orations, letters and poems. He is venerated as a saint and Doctor of the Church, and as one of the Three Holy Hierarchs.

Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335 – c. 394) was a Greek theologian and bishop of Nyssa in Cappadocia. With his elder brother Basil of Caesarea and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus, he is counted among the Cappadocian Fathers. He made important contributions to the doctrine of the Trinity and defended the Nicene faith. His philosophical thought shows the influence of Origen. Among his writings are the Life of Moses, homilies on the Song of Songs, Ecclesiastes, the Beatitudes and the Lord's Prayer, and the Life of Macrina. He is also known for his teaching on universal salvation and for condemning slavery outright.

Gregory of Tours (born Georgius Florentius, c. 538–594) was a Gallo-Roman bishop and historian. He served as Bishop of Tours from 573 during the Merovingian period. His major work is the Ten Books of Histories (Decem Libri Historiarum), often called the History of the Franks. It is the main source for Merovingian Gaul and has earned him the title "father of French history". He also wrote hagiographical works, including the Life of the Fathers (Vita Patrum) and books on the miracles of Martin of Tours and other saints.

Gregory Thaumaturgus ("the Wonderworker"), also called Gregory of Neocaesarea, was a Christian bishop of the third century (c. 213 – c. 270). He was born at Neocaesarea in Pontus and studied under Origen at Caesarea in Palestine. His farewell Panegyric to Origen describes Origen's way of teaching. He later became bishop of his native city, and later tradition credits him with many miracles. His writings include a Declaration of Faith, a paraphrase of Ecclesiastes, and a Canonical Epistle dealing with church discipline after the Gothic raids. He is venerated as a saint in the Catholic and Orthodox Churches.

Gregory the Great (c. 540–604) was bishop of Rome from 590 until his death. He was the son of a Roman senatorial family and served as prefect of the city. He then turned his family estate into a monastery and later acted as papal envoy at Constantinople. As pope he managed Rome's welfare and sent missionaries to England under Augustine of Canterbury. His writings include the Moralia on Job, the Pastoral Rule, the Dialogues and a large register of letters. He is counted among the four great Latin Church Fathers, and in the East he is known as "the Dialogist."

Gregory the Monk (Gregorius Monachus) was a tenth-century Byzantine monk who wrote in Greek, active in Constantinople around the middle of the century. He presented himself as a disciple of the holy man Basil the Younger and wrote Basil's Life. Besides Basil's miracles and prophecies, the long Life contains visionary narratives. The best known is the account of the dead servant Theodora passing through the aerial toll-houses, followed by Gregory's own vision of the Last Judgment. These sections later had a strong influence on Byzantine and Slavonic teaching about the afterlife. Little else is known of his life.

Gregory the Presbyter of Caesarea was a Byzantine Greek ecclesiastical writer about whom little is known. He was a priest of Caesarea, probably the city in Cappadocia. His dates are uncertain, though he is generally placed between the ninth and tenth centuries. He is known chiefly as the author of an encomium on the holy Fathers of the First Council of Nicaea (325), a rhetorical work praising the bishops who defended Nicene orthodoxy against Arianism. It is unclear whether he is the same person as other writers called Gregory the Presbyter.

Gundemar (Latin Gundemarus, died 612) was king of the Visigoths, ruling Hispania, Septimania and Galicia from 610 until his death in 612. He came to the throne after the murder of King Witteric. During his short reign he campaigned against the Basques and the Byzantine territories in southern Spain. A royal decree is preserved under his name. Issued with a synod of bishops held in Toledo, it confirmed Toledo as the metropolitan see of the province of Carthaginensis. This made it an early step in the city's rise as the leading church of Visigothic Spain. Sisebut succeeded him.

Hadoindus (also Hadoind), a Frankish churchman of the Merovingian period, was bishop of Le Mans in north-western Gaul. His episcopate is usually dated from about 623 until his death in 652. Only a small body of Latin writings survives under his name, chiefly documents connected with the administration and endowment of his church, among them his testament. They are valued less as literature than as evidence for the property, religious foundations and church government of the diocese of Le Mans in the seventh century.

Hadrian (Adrian) the Exegete was a Greek Christian writer, probably of the fifth century, about whom almost nothing is known personally. His dates are uncertain, though he is usually placed around the middle of that century. He is known for the Isagoge in sacras Scripturas (Introduction to the Divine Scriptures), a handbook explaining the Hebrew idioms, figures of speech and modes of expression found in the Bible. The work reflects the literal, historical method of the Antiochene school. Cassiodorus recommended it, and Photius also mentions it.

Hegemonius was a fourth-century Christian writer. Nothing is known of his life, and he is known only as the traditional, though doubtful, author of the Acta Archelai, which is why he is sometimes called Pseudo-Hegemonius. The work is the oldest and most important anti-Manichaean polemic. It was written in Greek, probably in the first half of the fourth century. It survives mainly in an early Latin translation, and large Greek portions are quoted in Epiphanius's Panarion. It tells of a fictional debate between Mani and Archelaus, bishop of Carchar in Mesopotamia. It sets out Manichaean cosmogony, gives a hostile account of Mani's life, and strongly shaped later anti-Manichaean writing.

Hegesippus (c. 107 – c. 180) was a Greek-writing Christian author of the second century. He was possibly a convert from Judaism. He travelled by way of Corinth to Rome, where he stayed during the time of Bishop Anicetus. He set out to show that the apostolic teaching had been handed down unbroken in the churches, and he wrote against Gnostic heresies and against Marcion. His five books of Hypomnemata ("Memoirs" or "Commentaries") are lost except for fragments, preserved mainly by Eusebius. These include his account of the martyrdom of James the Just and early material on the succession of bishops.

Hermas was a second-century Christian of Rome. He is the narrator and traditional author of The Shepherd of Hermas, an apocalyptic and moral work made up of Visions, Commandments (Mandates) and Similitudes (Parables). In it he describes himself as a former slave sold to a woman named Rhoda in Rome. The Muratorian fragment calls him the brother of Pius, bishop of Rome in the mid-second century. Some later writers identified him with the Hermas greeted in Romans 16:14, but that identification is not generally accepted. The Shepherd, which deals with repentance after baptism, was widely read and sometimes counted as scripture in the early Church.

Hermias, also called Hermias the Philosopher, was an obscure Christian apologist who wrote in Greek. Almost nothing is known of his life, and his date is uncertain. He is often placed in the third century, but some scholars date him as late as the fifth or sixth. His only surviving work is the Derision of Gentile Philosophers (Irrisio gentilium philosophorum), a short satire that sets the contradictory teachings of Greek philosophers on the soul, the world and first principles against one another. Taking Paul's claim that worldly wisdom is foolishness before God, he argues that philosophy comes from the apostasy of the angels.

Hesychius of Jerusalem, also called Hesychius the Priest, was a Greek Christian presbyter and biblical exegete active in Jerusalem in the first half of the fifth century. He probably died around 450, but almost nothing is known of his life. He wrote extensive commentaries on Scripture, especially the Psalms, as well as brief notes and divisions of the Twelve Prophets and Isaiah. Several homilies survive under his name, some on feasts and saints. His exegesis mostly follows the Alexandrian allegorical tradition. He should not be confused with the later bishop of Jerusalem of the same name.

Hesychius the Sinaite was a Greek monk associated with the monastic community of Mount Sinai. Tradition makes him abbot of the Monastery of the Burning Bush there. Almost nothing certain is known of his life, and his dates are disputed. He is usually placed somewhere between the seventh and ninth centuries. He is known for a collection of short chapters, arranged in centuries, called "On Watchfulness and Holiness" (De temperantia et virtute). It teaches watchfulness (nepsis), guarding the heart and constantly calling on the name of Jesus. The work was later included in the Philokalia and influenced the Byzantine hesychast tradition.

Jerome the Greek (Hieronymus Graecus) was an obscure Byzantine ecclesiastical writer. Almost nothing is known of his life, and his date is uncertain; he is usually placed somewhere between the seventh and ninth centuries. A few short Greek theological works are attributed to him, among them a dialogue on the Trinity and a treatise on the effect of baptism, along with other minor pieces. He is a different person from the Latin church father Jerome of Stridon, and his writings were sometimes confused with that Jerome's.

Hilarion the Georgian, also called Hilarion the Iberian (c. 822–875), was a Georgian monk from Kakheti who became a bishop at David Gareja. He was revered as a wonderworker and is venerated as a saint. According to his vita, he travelled to the Holy Land and visited Mount Tabor, the Jordan and the Lavra of Saint Sabas. He then lived as a hermit in a cave for seven years. In 864 he founded a monastery for Georgian monks on Mount Olympus in Bithynia. He died in Thessaloniki. Followers of Euthymius of Athos later wrote his Life on Mount Athos.

Hilary, often called Hilarius Gallus, was a Latin Christian in southern Gaul, probably a layman, who corresponded with Augustine of Hippo. Around 429 he wrote to Augustine at the same time as Prosper of Aquitaine. His letter survives as Letter 226 among Augustine's letters. In it he reported that monks and clergy around Marseille objected to Augustine's teaching on grace, predestination and perseverance, and he set out their arguments. Augustine answered with his treatises On the Predestination of the Saints and On the Gift of Perseverance. Little else is known of him.

Hilary of Arles (Hilarius Arelatensis, c. 403–449) was a Gallo-Roman bishop and saint. A relative of Honoratus, he gave up a secular career and became a monk at Lérins. In 429 he succeeded Honoratus as bishop of Arles. He was a strict, energetic metropolitan whose claims to authority across southern Gaul brought him into conflict with Pope Leo I, who restricted his jurisdiction in 445. His surviving writings include the Sermo de vita S. Honorati, a eulogy and life of his predecessor, and a letter to Eucherius of Lyon. His feast day is 5 May.

Hilary of Poitiers (Hilarius Pictaviensis; born early fourth century, died c. 367) was bishop of Poitiers in Gaul and the leading Latin opponent of Arianism. He was born into a pagan family and converted as an adult. In 356 the emperor Constantius II exiled him to Phrygia, where he came to know Greek theology at first hand. His major works include De Trinitate, De Synodis, a commentary on Matthew and the Tractatus super psalmos. He was also among the first Latin hymn writers. He is venerated as a saint and Doctor of the Church.

Hincmar (c. 806–882) was a Frankish churchman from a noble family of northern Francia. He was educated at the abbey of Saint-Denis and served as archbishop of Reims from 845 until his death. A jurist and theologian, he was a leading adviser and propagandist of Charles the Bald. He opposed Gottschalk of Orbais in the controversy over predestination and wrote on the divorce of Lothair II. He also wrote De ordine palatii and continued the Annals of Saint-Bertin. He clashed repeatedly with his nephew, Hincmar of Laon, and with the papacy over the rights of metropolitan bishops.

Hippolytus of Rome (c. 170 – c. 235) was a Greek-writing Christian theologian and biblical commentator. He was one of the most important Christian thinkers of his time, though his identity and the extent of his writings are uncertain. An older view holds that he led a rival community in Rome in opposition to its bishops and was later reconciled before dying a martyr. His works include the Treatise on Christ and Antichrist, Against Noetus and commentaries on Daniel. The Refutation of All Heresies and the Apostolic Tradition are also attributed to him, but both attributions are disputed.

Honoratus Antoninus was a fifth-century bishop of Constantina (ancient Cirta) in Roman Numidia, North Africa, active during the Vandal conquest. He is known for a single surviving work, the Epistola consolatoria ad Arcadium, written around 437. It is addressed to Arcadius, a Catholic exiled and later martyred under the Vandal king Gaiseric for refusing to accept Arianism. The letter urges him to stand firm in his confession of the Trinity and to endure suffering and death for Christ. It is a witness to the persecution of Catholics in Vandal Africa.

Hydatius (also Idatius or Idacius, c. 400 – c. 469) was a Latin chronicler and churchman from Gallaecia in northwestern Hispania. He became bishop of Aquae Flaviae, almost certainly modern Chaves in Portugal. His Chronicle continues Jerome's chronicle from 379 to about 468. It gives a gloomy, eyewitness account of the Suebic, Vandal and Visigothic invasions and settlements, and it is the main narrative source for fifth-century Hispania. A consular list, the Descriptio consulum, also known as the Consularia Constantinopolitana, is traditionally linked with his name.

Iakob Tsurtaveli (Jacob of Tsurtavi), also called Iakob Khutsesi ("the Priest"), was a fifth-century Georgian cleric from Tsurtavi, then the chief town of Gogarene in Lower Iberia. He served as personal priest to Queen Shushanik and was an eyewitness to her martyrdom at the hands of her husband, the bidaxsh Varsken, who had renounced Christianity. Jacob wrote the Martyrdom of the Holy Queen Shushanik, probably between 476 and 483. It is the oldest surviving work of Georgian literature. Almost nothing is known of his life beyond what he says in this work.

Abū al-Faraj ʿAbdallāh ibn al-Ṭayyib (died 1043) was a priest of the Church of the East, physician and philosopher in Baghdad. He served as secretary to the Catholicos and taught medicine at the ʿAḍudī hospital. Writing mainly in Arabic, he produced extensive commentaries on Aristotle and Galen within the Baghdad Aristotelian tradition. He also wrote biblical commentaries, notably the Firdaws al-Naṣrāniyya ("Paradise of Christianity"), compiled the canon-law collection Fiqh al-Naṣrāniyya and composed theological treatises. He is one of the leading Christian Arabic scholars of the eleventh century.

Ignatius of Antioch, also called Theophorus ("God-bearer"), was bishop of Antioch in the early second century and is counted among the Apostolic Fathers. Condemned to death, he was taken under guard to Rome. On the way he wrote seven letters: to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Romans, Philadelphians and Smyrnaeans, and to Polycarp of Smyrna. He was martyred in Rome, traditionally around 108, though the date is uncertain. His letters stress the authority of a single bishop, the unity of the church, the reality of Christ's flesh against docetism, the Eucharist, and his eagerness for martyrdom. They survive in shorter, longer and Syriac recensions, and scholars still debate which of these are authentic.

Ignatius the Deacon (c. 775 – after 845) was a Byzantine churchman and man of letters. He was a deacon and skeuophylax of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople and later became metropolitan of Nicaea. He is best known as a hagiographer, author of the Lives of the patriarchs Tarasius and Nicephorus, and as a poet, whose works include iambic verses, alphabetic poems, a short dramatic dialogue on the fall of Adam and Eve, and verse fables. A collection of his letters also survives. Together these writings are an important witness to the period of Iconoclasm and to the Byzantine literary revival of the ninth century.

Ioane Minchkhi was a tenth-century Georgian hymnographer and calligrapher. He lived at the same time as King George II of Abkhazia. He lived and worked at Mount Sinai, which is why many of his hymns survive in Sinai manuscripts. He is regarded as the author of the whole sticheron section of the first Georgian Lenten Triodion. Four of his hymns appear in the Iadgari (Tropologion) compiled by Michael Modrekili in 978–988. Scholars learned of his work through Ivane Javakhishvili, who found his hymns at Sinai in 1902. They included a canon to Saint George made up of 26 short hymns.

Ioane Sabanisdze (John Sabanisdze) was an eighth-century Georgian hagiographer active in Kartli, the region around Tbilisi, which was then under Arab Muslim rule. Little is known of his life beyond his single surviving work, the Martyrdom of Abo of Tiflis, written in about 786–790. It tells the story of Abo, a young Arab who converted to Christianity in Kartli and was executed at Tbilisi in 786. The text is one of the earliest original works of Georgian hagiography, and it presents Abo's steadfastness as an example to Georgian Christians living under Islamic rule.

Irenaeus of Lyon (c. 130–c. 202) was a Greek bishop and theologian. He came from Smyrna, where as a young man he heard Polycarp preach, and later became bishop of Lugdunum (Lyon) in Gaul. His main work, Against Heresies, written around 180, attacks Gnosticism, especially the Valentinian school. Against the Gnostic claim to secret knowledge, he pointed to Scripture, apostolic tradition and the succession of bishops. He is the earliest surviving writer to treat all four canonical gospels as essential. He is venerated as a saint and was named a Doctor of the Church in 2022.

Isaac of Antioch, also called Isaac of Amid, was a fifth-century Syriac writer and one of the major poets of Syriac literature. A large number of metrical homilies (memre) are attributed to him. Many stand out for their originality and cover ascetic, doctrinal and moral themes, including the end times, and some reflect events of his own day. His dates are uncertain. The Chronicle of Edessa puts his death in 451–452, while other accounts place it around 460. Modern scholars think the writings of more than one author named Isaac were later gathered under his name.

Isaac of Nineveh (c. 613 – c. 700), also called Isaac the Syrian, was a Syriac Christian bishop and ascetic writer of the Church of the East. Born in Beth Qatraye, on the Persian Gulf, he was made bishop of Nineveh but resigned after only about five months. He then lived as a solitary in the mountains of Khuzistan. His ascetical discourses on prayer, humility, stillness and divine love were translated into Greek at the monastery of Mar Saba and later into many other languages. They became deeply influential in Eastern Christian monasticism. He is venerated as a saint across several churches.

Isaiah the Abbot, also called Isaiah of Scetis, was a Greek-speaking monastic teacher of the fifth century who died around 489–491. He first lived as a monk at Scetis in Egypt. He later moved to Palestine and settled as a recluse near Gaza, where he guided disciples and was associated with the opponents of the Council of Chalcedon. His spiritual instructions were gathered as the Asceticon, a collection of discourses on ascetic practice, humility, the watch over thoughts and stillness (hesychia). It circulated widely in Greek, Syriac and other languages, and extracts were later included in the Philokalia.

Ishoʿyahb III of Adiabene (c. 580–659) was Patriarch, or Catholicos, of the Church of the East from 649 to 659. Before becoming patriarch he was a monk at Beth ʿAbe, then bishop of Nineveh (Mosul) and metropolitan of Adiabene (Erbil). More than one hundred of his Syriac letters survive, grouped according to these three offices. They are an important witness to Christian life in the first decades of Islamic rule and include letters to the Christians of Beth Qatraye in eastern Arabia. Tradition also credits him with reorganising the East Syriac liturgy.

Isidore of Pelusium (c. 360/370–c. 450) was a Greek-speaking Egyptian monk and ascetic. He came from a prominent Alexandrian family and lived as a monk near Pelusium, in the eastern Nile Delta, following the tradition of the Desert Fathers. He is known for a large body of letters to Cyril of Alexandria, Emperor Theodosius II and many others. About 2,000 of them were collected in antiquity at the monastery of the "Sleepless" monks in Constantinople. Most are brief, and many matter for the interpretation of Scripture, moral teaching and doctrinal debate. He is venerated as a saint on 4 February.

Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636) was a Hispano-Roman scholar, theologian and archbishop of Seville. He followed his brother Leander in that see and helped bring the Arian Visigothic monarchy into the Catholic Church. He had influence at the court of King Sisebut and took a leading part in the Councils of Toledo and Seville. His best-known work is the Etymologiae, an encyclopedia in twenty books that preserved much classical learning for the Middle Ages. He also wrote the Differentiae, on the distinctions between words, a world Chronicle, and historical and theological treatises. He is often called "the last scholar of the ancient world."

Jacob of Serugh (c. 451–521), also called Jacob of Sarug or Mar Jacob, was one of the foremost poets and theologians of Syriac Christianity, ranked second only to Ephrem the Syrian. He spent most of his career as a church official in the region of Serugh (modern Suruç, Turkey), and became bishop of Batnan in 519. He was a moderate Miaphysite. He is best known for his metrical homilies (memre), written in a twelve-syllable metre he devised. They cover biblical, liturgical and hagiographical subjects. Around 400 of the 763 works credited to him survive. Both Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian churches venerate him as a saint.

Jerome (Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus, c. 342/347–420) was a Latin priest, theologian, translator and historian. He was born at Stridon and later settled as a monk in Bethlehem. He is best known for his Latin translation of the Bible, later called the Vulgate, which Pope Damasus I commissioned. For the Old Testament he worked from the Hebrew rather than the Septuagint. He also wrote commentaries on Scripture and many letters. His other works include De viris illustribus and polemics against Helvidius, Rufinus and John of Jerusalem. He is honoured as one of the four great Latin Church Fathers.

Jingjing, known in Syriac as Adam, was an eighth-century monk and scholar of the Church of the East in Tang China. On the Syriac part of his inscription he calls himself priest, chorepiscopus and papash of China. He composed the text of the Xi'an Stele, set up in 781. Written in Chinese and Syriac, it records Christianity in China from the arrival of the missionary Alopen in 635. The Zunjing names him as the translator of thirty Jingjiao books. Many scholars also credit him with several of the other Chinese Christian texts known as the Jingjiao Documents.

Job the Monk (Latin Jobius Monachus) was a Greek Christian theologian, probably of the sixth century, although his exact dates and place of activity are uncertain. He is known mainly through the Patriarch Photius, who summarized a long treatise of his on the Incarnation in the Bibliotheca. Only fragments of his writings survive. They include a discussion of why the Son, rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit, became incarnate. His work belongs to the Christological debates that followed the Council of Chalcedon.

John Cassian (c. 360 – c. 435) was a monk and theologian honoured in both Western and Eastern churches. His birthplace is uncertain. As a young man he lived as a monk in Bethlehem and then among the desert monks of Egypt, where he was shaped by the teaching of Evagrius Ponticus. Later he founded monasteries near Marseille. His Institutes and Conferences brought the ideals and practices of Egyptian monasticism to the Latin West and deeply influenced Benedict's Rule. He also wrote On the Incarnation, against Nestorius. His views on grace and free will were later labelled "Semipelagian".

John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), "the Golden-mouthed", was a Greek Church Father, a preacher at Antioch, and from 398 Archbishop of Constantinople. His outspoken preaching against wealth and court luxury brought him into conflict with the Empress Eudoxia and Theophilus of Alexandria. He was deposed and died in exile. He is famed for his large body of homilies on books of the Bible, his treatise On the Priesthood, and his ascetic writings defending monasticism and opposing spiritual cohabitation. The Byzantine Divine Liturgy bears his name. He is honoured as one of the Three Holy Hierarchs.

John Climacus (c. 579 – c. 649), also called John of the Ladder, John Scholasticus and John Sinaites, was a Christian monk at the monastery on Mount Sinai, later Saint Catherine's Monastery. He is best known for the Ladder of Divine Ascent (Scala paradisi). He wrote it at the request of John, abbot of Raithu. Its thirty "steps" trace the monk's progress from renouncing the world to the highest virtues, and it became a foundational text of Eastern monastic spirituality. He also wrote a shorter work for superiors, To the Shepherd. He is venerated as a saint in both East and West.

John Geometres, also called Kyriotes, was a Byzantine poet, soldier and monk active in Constantinople in the second half of the tenth century. He died around 1000, and his birth date is uncertain. He served in the army before becoming a monk, and he is one of the leading literary figures of the Macedonian Renaissance. He wrote epigrams and other poems in verse, many of them on contemporary events. His prose works include orations, encomia and works on the Virgin Mary, among them hymns to the Theotokos and an oration on the Annunciation.

John I of Antioch was Patriarch of Antioch from about 429 until his death in 441 or 442. During the Nestorian controversy he led the moderate Eastern bishops and supported his friend Nestorius against Cyril of Alexandria. He reached the Council of Ephesus in 431 after Cyril had already opened it and condemned Nestorius. John then held a rival council that condemned Cyril. In 433 he made peace with Cyril on the basis of the Formula of Reunion, a compromise that cost him many supporters. Some of his letters and other writings from the controversy survive.

John IV, called Nesteutes or "the Faster" because of his strict asceticism, was patriarch of Constantinople from 582 until his death on 2 September 595. He was the first patriarch to take the title "Ecumenical Patriarch," which drew protests from Popes Pelagius II and Gregory the Great. Later tradition credits him with a penitential, a guide to confession and penance with its rite, and with homilies on penitence and abstinence. Scholars dispute whether he actually wrote these works. The Eastern Orthodox Church venerates him as a saint, and his feast falls on 2 September.

John Malalas (c. 491–578) was a Byzantine chronicler from Antioch in Syria. His surname probably comes from the Syriac word for "rhetor" or "orator". He seems to have moved later to Constantinople. He wrote the Chronographia, a world chronicle in eighteen books. It runs from the Creation to the reign of Justinian I, but its ending is lost. Written in Greek close to the everyday spoken language, it mixes biblical, mythological and imperial history, with particular attention to Antioch. It is the earliest surviving Byzantine world chronicle. Later chroniclers used it heavily, and it was translated into Old Church Slavonic.

John Mauropous (c. 1000 – c. 1080), whose name means "Blackfoot," was a Byzantine cleric, scholar, poet and hymnographer. He taught in Constantinople, where Michael Psellos was among his pupils, and was close to the court of Constantine IX Monomachos. He was later made Metropolitan of Euchaita in Asia Minor, and in his last years he retired to a monastery in the capital. His surviving works include epigrams and other poems, letters, orations and liturgical canons. He is traditionally credited with promoting the feast of the Three Holy Hierarchs: Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus and John Chrysostom.

John Maxentius (Joannes Maxentius) was a monk and theologian of the early sixth century and the leader of the so-called Scythian monks, a small group of Christological activists. Around 519–520 they promoted the Theopaschite formula "one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh" as a defence of the Council of Chalcedon against Nestorian readings. They pressed their case at Constantinople and before Pope Hormisdas in Rome, who did not endorse it. His Latin writings include letters, professions of faith and dialogues against the Nestorians. They also defend an Augustinian view of grace.

John Moschus (c. 550–619), also surnamed Eucrates, was a Byzantine monk and ascetical writer. He lived as a monk in Palestine, including at the monastery of Saint Theodosius near Jerusalem. With his friend and disciple Sophronius, later patriarch of Jerusalem, he travelled widely among the monastic communities of Palestine, Egypt, Syria and Sinai, and later went to Rome, where he died. He is known for the Spiritual Meadow (Pratum spirituale, Leimonarion), a collection of several hundred anecdotes and sayings of monks gathered on these travels. It is a major source for monastic life on the eve of the Arab conquests.

John of Arles (Ioannes Arelatensis) was a Latin churchman of sixth-century Gaul about whom little is known. He wrote a letter of spiritual counsel to the nuns of the monastery of Saint Mary at Arles, the community of consecrated women linked with Caesarius of Arles. The letter belongs to the ascetic and monastic tradition that took shape around Arles in the period after Caesarius. His exact dates, his office, and his relationship to the monastery are uncertain.

John of Biclaro (Iohannes Biclarensis, c. 540 – after 621) was a Catholic Visigothic chronicler and bishop of Girona. He was born at Scallabis in Lusitania and studied for many years in Constantinople. When he came back to Hispania, the Arian king Liuvigild exiled him for his Catholic faith. He then founded the monastery of Biclaro and wrote a rule for its monks, which has not survived. His chronicle continues that of Victor of Tunnuna and covers roughly 567 to 590. It is a key source for Visigothic Spain, and it ends with Reccared's conversion and the Third Council of Toledo (589).

John of Carpathus (Joannes Carpathius) was a Greek ascetic writer, probably of the seventh century, though his dates are uncertain. As his name suggests, he was linked to the Aegean island of Karpathos, between Crete and Rhodes, and he may have been its bishop. Little is known of his life. He is remembered for short spiritual chapters, above all a century of texts written to encourage monks "in India" who had written to him for counsel. These sayings deal with prayer, temptation, humility and perseverance. His writings were later included in the Philokalia.

John of Damascus (born Yuhanna ibn Mansur ibn Sarjun, c. 675/6–749) was a Christian monk, priest, hymnographer and theologian. He was born in Damascus under Umayyad rule and later became a monk, traditionally at Mar Saba near Jerusalem. He is best known for his three apologies defending holy images against iconoclasm.
