His Fount of Knowledge, which includes a treatise on heresies and the Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, summed up Greek patristic theology. He also wrote homilies on the Dormition and liturgical hymns, and is often called the last of the Greek Fathers.

John of Ephesus, also called John of Asia (c. 507 – c. 588), was a Miaphysite bishop and one of the earliest and most important historians to write in Syriac. He was born near Amida and became a monk there. Later, in Constantinople, he enjoyed Justinian's favour and led missions against paganism in Asia Minor. He was ordained bishop of Ephesus for the anti-Chalcedonian church, and under Justin II he was persecuted and imprisoned. His Ecclesiastical History, whose third part survives most fully, and his Lives of the Eastern Saints are major sources for the sixth century, including an eyewitness account of the Plague of Justinian.

John of Euboea was a Byzantine Greek preacher of the eighth century, active around the middle of that century, during the period of the iconoclast controversy. Little is known for certain about his life. Tradition associates him with John of Damascus, and he probably served as a monk or priest. Several Greek homilies survive under his name. The best known is a sermon on the Conception of the Theotokos, one of the earliest witnesses to that feast in the Byzantine Church. Another of his homilies deals with the Holy Innocents.

John of Jerusalem was a Byzantine Greek author, probably active in the tenth or eleventh century. He is known as the author of a Greek Life of Saint John of Damascus, the eighth-century monk, theologian and defender of icons. Little is known about his life. He is often identified with a patriarch of Jerusalem named John, but which one is uncertain, and so is the date of his work. His Vita is a main hagiographical source on John of Damascus and on the traditions that grew up around him in the medieval period.

John of Nicaea (Latin Joannes Nicaenus) was a Byzantine Greek churchman, traditionally described as archbishop of Nicaea in Bithynia. His dates are uncertain, though he is usually placed in the late eighth or ninth century. He is known for a short treatise or letter, De nativitate Domini, on the feast of Christ's Nativity. It defends celebrating Christmas on 25 December, separately from Epiphany, and is linked to Byzantine efforts to win the Armenian Church over to this practice. Little else is reliably known about his life.

John of Scythopolis, also called "the Scholasticus," was a Byzantine theologian and lawyer who was active in the second quarter of the sixth century. He served as bishop of Scythopolis (modern Beit She'an) in Palestine. A neo-Chalcedonian, he wrote treatises against Severus of Antioch and Eutyches that are now lost but were known to Photius. His lasting work is the earliest commentary on the writings of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite: a prologue and scholia on the treatises and letters. Many of these notes were later handed down under the name of Maximus the Confessor.

John Rufus, also called John of Beth Rufina or John of Maiuma (born c. 450), was an anti-Chalcedonian priest of Antioch and a disciple of Peter the Iberian. He was an ecclesiastical historian and may have become bishop of Maiuma, near Gaza. He wrote in Greek, but his works survive mainly in Syriac translation. They include the Life of Peter the Iberian, the Plerophoriae, a collection of stories and visions directed against the Council of Chalcedon, and the Commemoration of the Death of Theodosius. The Coptic Orthodox Church venerates him as John, Bishop of Gaza.

John the Archimandrite, also called Apa Johannes, was a Coptic monastic leader who headed the White Monastery near Sohag in Upper Egypt. Tradition counts him among the successors of Shenoute and Besa in leading that community. His dates are uncertain, but he probably lived sometime between the later fifth and the sixth century. He is known as the author of a set of monastic canons in Coptic. These rules continue the White Monastery's tradition of regulating community life, which Shenoute's own writings had established.

John the Deacon was a Byzantine Greek cleric and hagiographer of the late ninth and early tenth centuries. Little is known of his life beyond his authorship of a Life of Joseph the Hymnographer. Joseph was the Sicilian-born monk and prolific composer of liturgical canons who died in Constantinople in 886. John's biography, written after Joseph's death, is a principal source for the hymnographer's career. That career included his captivity, his support for icons during the Iconoclast controversy and his monastic and hymn-writing activity in the capital.

John the Deacon, also called Johannes Hymmonides (died c. 880), was a deacon of the Roman church and a Latin writer of the ninth century. He is best known for his Life of Pope Gregory the Great, in four books, which he wrote between about 873 and 876 at the request of Pope John VIII. It drew on Gregory's letters and other records kept in the papal archives. He also wrote a verse adaptation of the Cena Cypriani and started a life of Pope Clement I, which he left unfinished.

John the Deacon was a deacon of the Roman church active around 500. He is known for a Latin letter to Senarius, a high official at the Ostrogothic court of Theodoric. In it he answers questions about the rites of Christian initiation in Rome, including the catechumenate, the scrutinies, exsufflation, the giving of salt, anointing and baptism itself. The letter is an important witness to Roman baptismal liturgy before the early medieval sacramentaries. He is sometimes identified with the deacon John who later became Pope John I (523–526), but this is uncertain.

John the Iberian (Ioane Mtatsmindeli, died c. 1002) was a Georgian monk and Orthodox saint. He came from an aristocratic family of the principality of Tao-Klarjeti and took the monastic habit before settling on Mount Athos. Between about 980 and 983 he founded the Monastery of Iviron with his kinsman John Tornike. Iviron became the main centre of Georgian monasticism and learning on Athos. He was the father of Euthymius the Athonite. John taught his son Greek and Georgian, preparing him for his later work translating Greek texts into Georgian.

John the Monk (Ioannes Monachos) is the name attached to a number of Greek liturgical canons in Byzantine service books, including canons for the feasts of Saint Basil, John Chrysostom and the Apostle Peter. Who he was is uncertain. Byzantine tradition and some later scholars have identified him with John of Damascus, who was also a monk and hymnographer. Others think the name covers one or more separate hymnographers active between the eighth and tenth centuries. Nothing reliable is known about his life, and the attribution of individual hymns to him is often doubtful.

John the Solitary, also called John of Apamea (Syriac Yoḥannan Iḥidaya), was a Syriac Christian ascetic writer from Apamea in Syria, active in the first half of the fifth century. His spiritual teaching draws heavily on Evagrius Ponticus, whose works he read in Syriac translation. He is known for describing the spiritual life in stages of body, soul and spirit. His writings include letters, treatises and the Dialogue on the Soul. They became a major influence on later Syriac mysticism, especially on Isaac the Syrian in the seventh century.

John VIII Xiphilinus (c. 1010–1075) was a Byzantine jurist, scholar and churchman. Born in Trebizond, he became a leading legal figure in Constantinople and was known as an innovator in legal research. He was a friend of Michael Psellos. After a period as a monk, he served as Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 1064 until his death in 1075. He was the uncle of the monk John Xiphilinus, who made an epitome of Cassius Dio. Homilies circulate under the Xiphilinus name, but it is disputed whether uncle or nephew wrote them.

Joseph Hazzaya ("the Seer"), born about 710, was an 8th-century Syriac writer, ascetic and mystic of the Church of the East. He was born into a Zoroastrian Persian family near Nimrud and was taken captive as a child and sold into slavery. He later became a Christian and a monk. He lived as a hermit and served as abbot of the monasteries of Mar Bassima and Rabban Bakhtisho. He is said to have written 1,900 treatises, of which few survive. He is regarded as a systematizer of East Syriac mysticism, notably in his Letter on the Three Stages of the Monastic Life, which the manuscripts wrongly attribute to Philoxenus of Mabbug.

Joseph the Hymnographer (c. 816–886) was a Byzantine Greek monk and one of the most prolific liturgical poets of the Eastern Orthodox Church. Born in Sicily, he became a monk and later worked in Constantinople. He is remembered for opposing Iconoclasm. He wrote a great many canons, the nine-ode hymns sung at Matins, honouring the Theotokos and numerous saints. He also wrote a laudation of the Apostle Bartholomew. He is often confused with the older Joseph of Thessalonica, brother of Theodore the Studite, so many attributions of particular hymns to him are uncertain.

Flavius Josephus (born Yosef ben Mattityahu, c. 37 – c. 100) was a Jewish historian. He came from a priestly family in Jerusalem. During the First Jewish–Roman War he commanded the Jewish forces in Galilee and surrendered to Vespasian in 67. He later became a Roman citizen and a client of the Flavian emperors. He wrote in Greek. His works are The Jewish War, Antiquities of the Jews, an autobiographical Life and Against Apion, a defence of Judaism. They are major sources for Second Temple Judaism and the background of early Christianity, and Christian writers read and preserved them widely.

Joseppus is the otherwise unknown Greek Christian writer named as the author of the Hypomnesticon (Libellus memorialis), a handbook on the Old and New Testaments. Nothing certain is known of his life. His dates and place are disputed, though he is usually placed somewhere between the late fourth and the fifth century. The work is a compendium of short sections and lists in question-and-answer form, covering biblical people, genealogies, chronology and related subjects, along with notices on heresies. It is valued as evidence for early Christian biblical learning and reference literature.

Juansher Juansheriani was a Georgian prince (eristavi) and historian of the Chosroid royal house of Iberia, with lands in Inner Iberia and Kakheti. He is usually dated to about 790–800, though some place him in the 11th century. A note in medieval manuscripts of the Georgian Chronicles (Kartlis Tskhovreba) names him, as husband of a niece of Archil of Kakheti, as author of the Life of Vakhtang Gorgasali. This history of Iberia runs from Vakhtang I to Archil. The attribution is disputed, and some scholars have assigned much of the work to Leonti Mroveli.

Julian of Eclanum (c. 386 – c. 455) was bishop of Eclanum, near Benevento in southern Italy, and the leading theologian of the later Pelagian movement. In 418 he refused to sign Pope Zosimus's condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius. He was deposed and exiled as a result. He then carried on a long written controversy with Augustine of Hippo, attacking his teaching on original sin, grace, concupiscence and marriage. Augustine answered him in Contra Julianum and the unfinished Opus imperfectum. Julian also wrote commentaries on Hosea, Joel and Amos, which were once attributed to Rufinus.

Julianus Pomerius was a Latin Christian writer of the late fifth century. Born in North Africa (Mauretania), he settled in Gaul and taught rhetoric at Arles. There he was ordained priest and became a teacher of the young Caesarius of Arles. He wrote five treatises, but only De vita contemplativa survives. It is a work in three books on the contemplative and active life, the duties of clergy, and the virtues and vices. For centuries it was wrongly attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine. It draws on Augustine and influenced later medieval thought about pastoral care. He probably died around 500.

Sextus Julius Africanus (c. 160 – c. 240) was a Christian traveller, scholar and historian who wrote in Greek and was connected with Palestine, especially Emmaus (Nicopolis). His five-book Chronography, which survives only in fragments, set biblical and pagan history side by side, counting from creation to the third century. Eusebius and the later Byzantine chroniclers drew heavily on it. He also wrote the Kestoi, a miscellany on many subjects. Two of his letters are known: one to Origen questioning whether the story of Susanna is authentic, and one to Aristides reconciling the genealogies of Jesus in Matthew and Luke.

Junillus Africanus was a Latin-speaking layman of North African origin, active in the 540s. He served at Constantinople as quaestor of the sacred palace under Emperor Justinian I, succeeding Tribonian. He is known for the Instituta regularia divinae legis, a handbook of biblical study in two books, written as questions and answers. It was dedicated to the African bishop Primasius of Hadrumetum. The work drew on the teaching of Paul the Persian of the School of Nisibis. Through it, Western readers came to know the Antiochene method of exegesis associated with Theodore of Mopsuestia.

Justin Martyr (c. 100–c. 165), also called Justin the Philosopher, was an early Christian apologist. He was born at Flavia Neapolis in Samaria and later taught in Rome. In his First and Second Apologies he defends Christians against persecution and describes their worship. The First Apology is addressed to Emperor Antoninus Pius. His Dialogue with Trypho argues with a Jewish interlocutor that Christ fulfils the Hebrew Scriptures. Justin taught that the divine Logos was at work before the incarnation, so that philosophers such as Socrates partly shared in the truth. He was martyred in Rome under Marcus Aurelius.

Justinian I, called the Great (c. 482–565), was Roman emperor at Constantinople from 527 to 565. His generals won back North Africa, Italy and part of Spain. He ordered the codification of Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis and built the Hagia Sophia. He was a Chalcedonian Christian who was closely involved in church affairs. He wrote theological treatises and edicts, including a treatise against Origen and writings condemning Theodore of Mopsuestia in the Three Chapters controversy. That controversy led to the Second Council of Constantinople, which he called in 553.

Justus of Urgell (died after 546) was a Hispano-Roman bishop and saint, the first recorded bishop of Urgell in the north-east of the Iberian Peninsula. He took part in the Second Council of Toledo in 527 and in the councils of Lleida and Valencia in 546. He wrote a short allegorical commentary on the Song of Songs, which he dedicated in a covering letter to Sergius, bishop of Tarragona. Isidore of Seville included him among his illustrious men and names his three brothers, Nebridius, Elpidius and Justinian, as bishops. His feast falls on 28 May.

Gaius Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus (fl. c. 330) was a Latin Christian poet from Hispania. Jerome describes him as a priest of very noble family. Around 329–330, in the reign of Constantine, he wrote the Evangeliorum libri quattuor. This paraphrase of the Gospel narrative in about 3,200 Virgilian hexameters follows mainly Matthew and is generally regarded as the first Christian Latin epic. It was widely read and imitated, became a school text, and was well known throughout the Middle Ages, including in the British Isles.

Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was a Latin Christian rhetorician and apologist from North Africa, said to have been a pupil of Arnobius. Diocletian appointed him to teach rhetoric at Nicomedia. Later he became an adviser to Constantine I and tutor to Constantine's son Crispus. His main work, the Divine Institutes, argues for the reasonableness and truth of Christianity against pagan critics. He also wrote On the Anger of God and On the Deaths of the Persecutors, and the poem The Phoenix is often attributed to him. Renaissance humanists admired his polished style and called him the "Christian Cicero."

Leander of Seville (c. 534 – 600 or 601) was a Hispano-Roman bishop of Seville and the elder brother of Isidore of Seville, who succeeded him. He helped bring the Visigothic royal family from Arianism to Catholicism, first Hermenegild and then King Reccared. He presided over the Third Council of Toledo (589) and closed it with a homily in praise of the Church. In Constantinople he became a friend of the future Pope Gregory the Great, who dedicated his Moralia in Job to him. He also wrote a rule for virgins addressed to his sister Florentina.

Leo Grammaticus was a Byzantine Greek scribe and chronicler of the early eleventh century. A Chronographia that he completed in 1013 bears his name. It is a world chronicle running from the Creation to the reign of Romanos I Lekapenos in the mid-tenth century. Modern scholars regard it as a version of the chronicle tradition linked to Symeon Logothete, and Leo appears to have been its copyist or redactor rather than its original author. Almost nothing else is known about his life.

Leo III the Isaurian (c. 685–741), also called the Syrian, was Byzantine emperor from 717 until his death and founded the Isaurian dynasty. His reign ended the Twenty Years' Anarchy, a period of rapid changes of ruler. He drove back the Umayyad siege of Constantinople in 717–718 and went on to defend the empire against the Arabs. He is best known for starting Byzantine iconoclasm by forbidding the veneration of icons. With his son Constantine V he issued the Ecloga, a short Greek law code that revised Justinian's legislation. He also issued novels (new laws).

Leo of Ohrid (died 1056) was a Byzantine churchman who served as Archbishop of Ohrid from 1037 until his death. Before that he had been chartophylax of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. He is best known for his letters against the azymes, written around 1053 with the backing of Patriarch Michael Cerularius and addressed to Bishop John of Trani in southern Italy. In them he attacked Latin customs, above all the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist, as well as fasting on Saturdays. The letters provoked replies from Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida and contributed to the tensions behind the East–West Schism of 1054.

Leo of Sens (Latin Leo Senonensis, died 541) was bishop of Sens in Merovingian Gaul from about 533 until his death. Little is known of his life. One letter of his survives, addressed to the Frankish king Childebert I. In it Leo protests against the king's plan to set up a separate bishopric at Melun, a town within the diocese of Sens, which he regarded as a breach of canonical order. The letter is a small but useful witness to relations between Frankish kings and bishops in the sixth century. He is venerated locally as a saint.

Leo the Deacon (Leo Diaconus) was a Byzantine Greek historian born around 950 at Kaloe in Asia Minor. He was educated in Constantinople and served as a deacon in the imperial palace. His History in ten books covers the reigns of Romanos II, Nikephoros II Phokas and John I Tzimiskes, and the early years of Basil II, and often draws on what he saw himself. He wrote in a classicizing style modelled on Homer and on historians such as Agathias. He is best known for his eyewitness portrait of Sviatoslav I of Kiev during the Rus'–Byzantine war over Bulgaria.

Leo I, called Leo the Great (died 461), was a Roman aristocrat who served as bishop of Rome from 440 until his death. His birth date is uncertain and is usually put around 400 or earlier. He did much to develop the idea of papal authority, which he based on the succession of Rome's bishops from Saint Peter. His Tome, a letter written in 449, set out the doctrine of Christ's two natures, divine and human, united in one person. The Council of Chalcedon accepted it in 451. In 452 he met Attila the Hun, who then turned back from Italy. Nearly a hundred sermons and many letters by him survive. He is a Doctor of the Church.

Leo VI the Wise (866–912) was Byzantine emperor from 886 to 912 and the second ruler of the Macedonian dynasty, though his parentage is unclear. He was educated by the patriarch Photius and was known for his learning. His reign carried on the revival of letters begun by Basil I. It saw the completion of the Basilika law code and his own Novels. He wrote homilies and orations, letters, religious poetry and the military treatise known as the Tactica. His reign also included military setbacks against Bulgaria and the Arabs. His fourth marriage set off a serious conflict with the Church.

Leonti Mroveli, also called Leontius of Ruisi, was a Georgian chronicler, probably an ecclesiastic. "Mroveli" means "of Ruisi," and he was most likely bishop or archbishop of that diocese. He is usually placed in the eleventh century, since a Leonti of Ruisi is recorded in an inscription of 1066, but earlier datings to the eighth century have also been proposed. He is credited with the Lives of the Kings of Kartli and related texts in the Georgian Chronicles (Kartlis Tskhovreba). Scholars disagree on whether he wrote these texts or only compiled them from older material. His work moved Georgian literature toward secular history.

Leontius of Byzantium (c. 485–c. 543) was a Greek monk and theologian who defended the Christology of the Council of Chalcedon during the controversies of the sixth century. Little is known about his life, though he is usually linked with Palestinian monasticism and with Origenist circles. His main work, Against the Nestorians and Eutychians, along with the Solution of the Arguments of Severus and the Thirty Chapters, uses Aristotelian logical definitions to explain how Christ's two natures are united in one hypostasis. Some works attributed to him, notably De sectis, are of doubtful authenticity.

Leontius of Jerusalem was a Greek monk and theologian of the sixth century, active around the 530s and 540s. His dates are debated, and he is known only from his writings. He defended the Council of Chalcedon at a time when much of Egypt, Palestine and Syria rejected it. He wrote two treatises, Contra Monophysitas and Contra Nestorianos. In them he tried to convince opponents of Chalcedon that its Christology was valid. He was long confused with his contemporary Leontius of Byzantium, and several anti-heretical works passed down under the name "Leontius" belong to that author or to others.

Leontius of Neapolis (c. 590 – c. 668) was a seventh-century bishop of Neapolis, modern Limassol, in Cyprus, and a Greek hagiographer and apologist. Arcadius, archbishop of Constantia, commissioned him to write a Life of John the Merciful, patriarch of Alexandria. He also wrote a Life of Symeon the Holy Fool, along with sermons and a lost Life of Spyridon. His apology against the Jews defended the Christian veneration of images. Fragments of it survive through John of Damascus and the Second Council of Nicaea of 787. His lively style is valued as evidence for vernacular Byzantine Greek.

Leontius was a Greek-writing presbyter and monk of a monastery of St Sabas, usually identified as the Greek community of San Saba in Rome. He is known only as the author of the Life of Gregory of Agrigentum, a long hagiographical account of the sixth-century bishop of Agrigento in Sicily, covering his travels, his time in Rome and Constantinople, and the accusations brought against him. Little else is known of Leontius, and his date is disputed. Estimates range from the seventh to the ninth century.

Leporius was a Latin monk and priest of the early fifth century. In Gaul he taught a Christology that separated the divine Word from the man Jesus, a view later seen as anticipating Nestorianism, and he was also accused of Pelagian-leaning opinions. After he was censured by Gallic bishops, he went to North Africa. There, under Augustine of Hippo and Aurelius of Carthage, he retracted his views. His Libellus emendationis, addressed to the bishops of Gaul, records this retraction and was later cited as a statement of orthodox teaching on the Incarnation. He afterwards served as a priest at Hippo.

Liberatus of Carthage was a sixth-century archdeacon of the church of Carthage in Roman North Africa. He belonged to the African clergy who opposed Emperor Justinian's condemnation of the Three Chapters. He is known for his Breviarium causae Nestorianorum et Eutychianorum, written in Latin probably between about 555 and 566. It is a concise history of the Nestorian and Monophysite controversies, running from the ordination of Nestorius to the mid-sixth century. Because it draws on documents and Greek sources that are now partly lost, it remains a valuable account of the Christological disputes surrounding the councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon.

Licinianus was bishop of Carthago Nova (Cartagena) in the late sixth century, when the city belonged to the Byzantine province of Spania. Three Latin letters by him survive. In one he writes to Pope Gregory the Great, praising his Pastoral Rule and raising the problem of ordaining poorly educated clergy. Another, to the deacon Epiphanius, argues that the soul and angels are incorporeal. The third, to Bishop Vincent of Ibiza, rejects a supposed letter from heaven about keeping Sunday. According to Isidore of Seville, he died at Constantinople, reportedly poisoned, around 602.

Lucian was a priest of Caphargamala, a village near Jerusalem, in the early fifth century. In 415 he reported a series of dreams in which Gamaliel, the teacher of the apostle Paul, revealed where the relics of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, Nicodemus, Gamaliel and his son Abibas were buried. Bishop John II of Jerusalem oversaw the excavation, and Stephen's relics were moved to the church of Holy Sion. Lucian's Greek letter describing the discovery spread quickly through a Latin version by the priest Avitus of Braga, and it helped the cult of Stephen grow across the Christian world.

Lucifer of Cagliari (died c. 370–371) was bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia and a fierce opponent of Arianism. At the Council of Milan in 355 he refused to condemn Athanasius and was exiled by Emperor Constantius II. In exile he wrote vehement Latin polemics addressed to the emperor, including De non conveniendo cum haereticis, De regibus apostaticis, De non parcendo in Deum delinquentibus and Moriendum esse pro Dei filio. In 362 he consecrated Paulinus as bishop of Antioch, which deepened the schism there. His rigorist followers became known as Luciferians, and he is venerated as a saint in Sardinia.

Luculentus was a Latin Christian writer about whom almost nothing is known. Even his dates are uncertain: he is usually placed somewhere between the sixth and eighth centuries, and neither his homeland nor his church office is recorded. The only work attributed to him is a set of short commentaries, or homily-like explanations, on passages from the New Testament, mostly Gospel readings. These are known by the title In aliquot Novi Testamenti partes commentarii. The work is a modest example of early medieval Latin biblical interpretation, drawing on earlier patristic exegesis.

Lupus of Troyes (c. 383 – c. 478) was a Gallic bishop who led the see of Troyes for about fifty years. Before becoming bishop he was a monk at Lérins. In the late 420s, when the bishops of Britain asked the Gallic church for help against Pelagianism, he and Germanus of Auxerre were sent to the island. According to tradition, he later saved Troyes from Attila's Huns in 451. A small number of his letters survive. He was a friend and correspondent of Sidonius Apollinaris, who greatly respected him, and is venerated as a saint.

Macarius of Egypt (c. 300–391), also called Macarius the Great or the Elder, was an Egyptian monk and hermit. He is traditionally regarded as a disciple of Antony the Great and as the founder of the monastic settlement at Scetis (Wadi El Natrun), where he later served as a priest. Many sayings attributed to him are preserved in the Apophthegmata Patrum. The influential Fifty Spiritual Homilies and related writings have long circulated under his name, but most scholars now assign them to an anonymous Syrian author, known as Pseudo-Macarius.

Magnus Maximus (c. 335–388) was Roman emperor in the West from 383 to 388. He was born in Gallaecia and served as an officer in Britain under Theodosius the Elder. His troops proclaimed him emperor in Britain in 383, and he overthrew Gratian, ruling from Trier with the support of Gaul. He presented himself as a defender of Nicene orthodoxy, and his reign saw the trial and execution of Priscillian. His letter to Pope Siricius survives. He invaded Italy in 387, and Theodosius I defeated and executed him in 388.

Malchion was a presbyter of Antioch in the later third century, under the emperors Claudius II and Aurelian. He was a learned rhetorician who headed a school of rhetoric in the city. Eusebius records that at the synod of Antioch around 268 or 269 he debated the bishop Paul of Samosata and exposed his views, which led to Paul's condemnation and deposition. Malchion is credited with writing the synod's letter against Paul to the bishops of Rome and Alexandria, and Jerome gives him an entry in On Illustrious Men.

Mappinius (also Mapinius) was bishop of Reims from about 535 to 550, during the Merovingian period. His name is of Gaulish origin. He sent the archdeacon Protadius to represent him at the Fifth Council of Orléans in 549. Two of his letters survive in the Epistulae Austrasicae. In one he congratulates Bishop Vilicus of Metz on his seventieth birthday and asks about the price of pigs. In the other he writes to Nicetius of Trier to excuse his absence from the Council of Toul in 550, and the letter is a valuable source for that council.

Mara bar Serapion was a Stoic philosopher from Samosata in the Roman province of Syria. He is known only from a single letter, written in Syriac to his son Serapion while he was held captive. The letter was written after the Roman annexation of Samosata in AD 72 but before the third century. Many scholars place it soon after AD 73, while others prefer the later second century. It urges the pursuit of wisdom and cites the unjust deaths of Socrates, Pythagoras and "the wise king of the Jews." Many scholars read the last as an early non-Christian reference to Jesus, but this remains debated.

Marcellinus Comes (died c. 534) was a Latin chronicler of the Eastern Roman Empire. He was an Illyrian by birth and spent most of his life at the court in Constantinople, where he served as cancellarius to Justinian before Justinian became emperor. His only surviving work is the Chronicle, which continues Jerome's chronicle from 379 to 518 and was later extended to 534. It is ordered by indictions and consular years and deals mainly with events in the East. The Chronicle is valued for its contemporary account of the period and is often cited for dating the end of the Western Empire to 476.

Marcellinus was a Latin presbyter of the Luciferian party, the rigorist group named after Lucifer of Cagliari. It refused communion with Arians and with Nicene clergy who had compromised with them. In 383 or 384 he and the presbyter Faustinus travelled to Constantinople to petition Emperor Theodosius I. Their joint petition, the Libellus precum, complains of the persecution of their community, including by supporters of Pope Damasus. It is an important statement of Luciferian belief. Theodosius answered with a rescript, the Lex augusta, granting them protection. Little else is known of Marcellinus.

Marcellus of Ancyra (died c. 374) was bishop of Ancyra in Galatia. He attended the Synod of Ancyra and the First Council of Nicaea and was a firm opponent of Arianism. His treatise against Asterius the Sophist stressed the strict unity of God. Opponents accused him of a modified Sabellianism, and he was deposed in 336. Pope Julius and the Council of Serdica later restored him, but his teaching remained controversial. His writings survive mainly as fragments quoted by Eusebius of Caesarea. His letter to Pope Julius is preserved by Epiphanius.

Marius Mercator (c. 390 – shortly after 451) was a Latin Christian writer, probably from North Africa. He was a supporter of Augustine of Hippo, and around 418 he wrote anti-Pelagian treatises in Rome that he sent to Augustine. From 429 until about 448 he lived in Constantinople. There his Commonitorium on Caelestius helped bring about the expulsion of Caelestius and Julian of Eclanum from the city and their condemnation at Ephesus in 431. He also wrote against Nestorius, and he translated and compiled excerpts from Greek writers, among them Nestorius, Cyril of Alexandria, Theodore of Mopsuestia and Theodoret.

Marius of Avenches (Marius Aventicensis, c. 532–596; some accounts give 530–594) was a Gallo-Roman bishop of Aventicum, modern Avenches in Switzerland, from 574. He is remembered for his brief Latin chronicle. It continues the chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine and covers the years from 455 to 581. Terse, year-by-year entries record events in Burgundy, Frankish Gaul, Italy and the Eastern Empire. It is a valuable source for the post-Roman West in the sixth century. He died at Lausanne, where he was later venerated as a saint, with his feast kept on 9 or 12 February.

Gaius Marius Victorinus, also called Victorinus Afer, was a fourth-century Latin rhetorician, grammarian and Neoplatonic philosopher. He was born in Roman Africa and taught rhetoric with great distinction in Rome. Around 355, late in life, he converted from paganism to Christianity, a conversion Augustine describes in the Confessions. He gave up teaching after Julian's edict of 362 barred Christians from teaching. His Latin translations of Aristotle and of Neoplatonic writings influenced Augustine. As a Christian he wrote philosophical treatises against Arianism and the earliest surviving Latin commentaries on Paul's letters. Several minor works attributed to him are of doubtful authenticity.

Mark of Monte Cassino (Marcus Cassinensis) was a Latin poet of the later sixth century, or perhaps the early seventh, linked to the monastery of Monte Cassino. Almost nothing is known of his life. Paul the Deacon names him as a disciple of Benedict of Nursia, but his exact dates are uncertain. He is known for a short poem in honour of Saint Benedict, the Carmen de Sancto Benedicto. It celebrates Benedict's arrival at Monte Cassino and the founding of his monastery there, and it is among the earliest literary witnesses to devotion to the saint.

Mark the Deacon (Marcus Diaconus) was an early fifth-century Christian hagiographer from the province of Asia. He worked as a calligrapher in Jerusalem, where he entered the service of Porphyrius around 395, and followed him to Gaza when Porphyrius became its bishop. There he became a deacon and supported the campaign to close the city's pagan temples. His Life of Porphyry, Bishop of Gaza, is a vivid account of how Gaza became Christian. It survives in Greek, Latin and Georgian versions. Scholars debate its historical reliability and how the Greek text was transmitted.

Mark the Hermit, also called Mark the Ascetic (Marcus Eremita), was a Greek Christian ascetic writer and saint of the fifth century. Little is certain about his life, and his exact dates and place of activity are disputed. Tradition calls him a disciple of John Chrysostom. His writings are practical rather than speculative and deal with the monastic and spiritual life. They include On the Spiritual Law and On Those Who Think They Are Justified by Works, both later included in the Philokalia. He also wrote on baptism and against Nestorian Christology.

Martin of Braga, also called Martin of Dume (c. 518–580), was a monk, missionary and bishop in Gallaecia in north-western Iberia. He was born in Pannonia and founded the monastery of Dumium. He then became bishop there and later archbishop of Braga, where he presided over the Second Council of Braga in 572. He is honoured as the "Apostle to the Suevi" for bringing the Suebic kingdom to Chalcedonian Christianity. Gregory of Tours praised his learning. His writings include De correctione rusticorum, a sermon against rural paganism, and short moral treatises in the Senecan tradition, such as the Formula vitae honestae.

Martin of Tours (316/336–397) was the third bishop of Tours and one of the most venerated saints of the Latin West. Born at Savaria in Pannonia, he served in the Roman cavalry in Gaul before leaving the army and becoming a disciple of Hilary of Poitiers. He founded a monastery at Ligugé and became bishop of Tours in 371. He promoted Nicene Christianity but opposed the violent persecution of the Priscillianists. His Life by Sulpicius Severus made famous the story of his dividing his cloak with a beggar. A short confession of faith on the Trinity is attributed to him, but its authenticity is doubtful.

Vettius Agorius Basilius Mavortius (active 527–534) was a Roman aristocrat of the senatorial class who lived under Ostrogothic rule in Italy and served as consul in 527. He was one of the learned laymen who kept classical literary culture alive in sixth-century Rome. A subscription records that he corrected a manuscript of Horace. A Virgilian cento, De ecclesia, which reuses lines of Virgil to describe Christian worship, has been ascribed to him, but the attribution is uncertain.

Maximus of Jerusalem, often counted as Maximus II, was a Christian bishop of Jerusalem (Aelia Capitolina) active about 185–196. According to Jerome, he lived under the emperors Commodus and Septimius Severus. Jerome also says he wrote on the origin of evil and on whether matter was made by God. Eusebius ascribes a treatise On Matter to him and quotes a passage from it. That passage closely matches Methodius of Olympus's dialogue On Free Will, so who actually wrote it is uncertain. He is distinct from the earlier Maximus I and from Maximus III, bishop from 333 to 347.

Maximus of Turin was a Latin bishop and preacher, the first known Bishop of Turin in northern Italy. His dates are disputed. Gennadius places his death under Honorius and Theodosius II, around 408–423. Other accounts identify him with a Maximus who signed at councils in 451 and 465, which would give him a much longer life. He is known for a large collection of sermons on the liturgical year, the saints and local martyrs, and the moral life of his congregation. They also show lingering pagan practices and the disruption caused by barbarian invasions.

Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662) was a Byzantine monk and theologian. Before becoming a monk he was a civil servant at the court of Emperor Heraclius. He became the leading opponent of Monothelitism, defending the Chalcedonian teaching that Christ has both a divine and a human will. He was tried, his tongue and right hand were mutilated, and he died in exile in Lazica, in present-day Georgia. The Third Council of Constantinople (680–681) upheld his theology. His works include the Ambigua, the Mystagogia, and writings on asceticism and the spiritual life.

Meletius the Monk (Meletius Monachus) was a Byzantine Greek monk and writer. Almost nothing is known of his life, and his dates are uncertain. He is usually placed somewhere between the ninth and eleventh centuries. He is known for a treatise On the Nature of Man (De natura hominis). It describes the structure of the human body from head to foot, and it combines medical learning drawn from Galen and other ancient physicians with Christian theological and scriptural reflection on humanity as God's creation. The work is a notable witness to Byzantine medical and anthropological thought.

Melito of Sardis (died c. 180) was bishop of Sardis in western Asia Minor and one of the leading Christian figures in Roman Asia in the second century. Most of his many writings are lost. They included an Apology addressed to Emperor Marcus Aurelius, and fragments of his works survive in quotations by Eusebius and others. He is remembered for the earliest known Christian list of Old Testament books. His homily Peri Pascha (On the Pascha) was recovered in the twentieth century and is an important witness to Quartodeciman Easter preaching. Polycrates of Ephesus records that he was buried at Sardis.

Memnon was metropolitan bishop of Ephesus when the Third Ecumenical Council met in his city in 431. He was a firm ally of Cyril of Alexandria against Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, and helped make sure the council condemned Nestorius and upheld the title Theotokos for the Virgin Mary. A rival assembly of Eastern bishops led by John of Antioch declared him deposed, and he was held in custody for a time, but he kept his see. A few of his letters and other short writings from the controversy survive in the council's acts.

Flavius Merobaudes was a 5th-century Latin poet and rhetorician of Frankish descent who was raised in Spain. He served as court poet to Valentinian III and the general Aetius, and he also campaigned as a soldier. In 435 a statue was set up in his honour at Rome, and its inscription praises him as both warrior and poet. Parts of his panegyrics and shorter poems survive in a palimpsest at St Gall. The short hexameter poem De Christo is credited to him in one manuscript and to Claudian in another, so its authorship is disputed.

Methodius I (c. 788/800–847) was a Byzantine churchman and Patriarch of Constantinople from 843 until his death. Born in Syracuse in Sicily, he became a monk and a leading defender of icons, and was imprisoned under the iconoclast emperors. After the death of Emperor Theophilos he was made patriarch with the support of the Empress Theodora. In 843 he presided over the restoration of icon veneration, which ended the second period of Byzantine Iconoclasm and is commemorated as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. His writings include hagiography, hymns and short ecclesiastical works. He is venerated as a saint, with his feast on 14 June.

Methodius of Olympus (died c. 311) was an early Christian bishop, theological writer and martyr, traditionally linked with Olympus in Lycia in Asia Minor. He is best known for the Banquet of the Ten Virgins, or Concerning Chastity, a dialogue modelled on Plato's Symposium that praises virginity. He was one of the earliest critics of Origen. His dialogue On the Resurrection rejects Origen's views on the resurrection body. Other works include Concerning Free-Will, a writing against Porphyry and exegetical pieces, several surviving only in fragments or Old Church Slavonic translation. He is venerated as a saint.

Michael I Cerularius (Keroularios; c. 1000–1059) was Patriarch of Constantinople from 1043 until Emperor Isaac I Komnenos deposed him in 1058. He died in exile the following year. He strongly opposed Latin church practices, especially the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist. This led to a sharp dispute with Pope Leo IX. In 1054 the papal legate Cardinal Humbert excommunicated him, and his synod answered with a counter-anathema in a synodal edict. These events are usually treated as the start of the Great Schism between the Eastern and Western churches. His canonical decrees and letters also survive.

Michael Synkellos (c. 760–846) was an Arab Christian priest, monk and saint who wrote in Greek. He served as synkellos of the patriarchate of Jerusalem (c. 811–815) and later of Constantinople (843–846). He took part in disputes over the filioque and opposed Byzantine iconoclasm, which left him imprisoned from 815 to 843. Despite this, he wrote widely. His works include a treatise on Greek syntax, theological writings, hagiography such as an encomium of Dionysius the Areopagite, hymns and poetry. He also made at least one translation from Arabic.

Mikael Modrekili was a Georgian monk, calligrapher, hymnographer and liturgical scholar of the 10th century. His epithet is usually rendered "the bent", and is also understood as "the hermit" or "simple monk". At the monastery of Shatberdi, between 978 and 988, he worked with two anonymous copyists to compile and copy a large tropologion, or Iadgari. This hymn collection gathers the original and translated Georgian chants known in his time and includes early musical neumes. He was also an anthologist and poet. His nephew, Ioane Berai, was a calligrapher at Shatberdi too.

Marcus Minucius Felix was a Roman lawyer and one of the earliest Latin apologists for Christianity. He was probably active in the late second or early third century, and he is traditionally said to have died in Rome around 250. His precise dates are uncertain, and so is his relationship to Tertullian, whose Apologeticum closely parallels his work. His only surviving work is the Octavius, a dialogue in polished Ciceronian Latin. In it the Christian Octavius Januarius answers the pagan Caecilius Natalis, rejecting popular accusations against Christians and arguing for monotheism and providence. By the end Caecilius is persuaded to convert.

Modestus of Jerusalem (died c. 634) was a Greek churchman in Palestine. He was abbot of the monastery of Saint Theodosius. After the Persians took Jerusalem in 614 and carried Patriarch Zacharias into captivity, Modestus ran the church there as locum tenens and restored its damaged shrines, including the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. When Zacharias died, Modestus succeeded him as patriarch, serving for a short time around 632–634. Several homilies have come down under his name, among them an encomium on the Dormition of the Virgin, though scholars dispute whether it is really his. He is venerated as a saint in East and West.

Montanus was bishop of Toledo in Visigothic Spain in the early sixth century, active roughly 522–531. As metropolitan he presided over the Second Council of Toledo, held in 527 or 531, which dealt chiefly with Arianism and is the first council to identify Toledo as a metropolitan see. Two of his Latin letters survive. One, to the clergy and people of the Palencia region, condemns Priscillianism and irregular church practices. The other, to the monk Turibius, praises his work against that heresy. Ildefonsus of Toledo later included Montanus in his De viris illustribus.

Moses bar Kepha (c. 813 or c. 833–903), also called Mushe bar Kipho, was one of the most celebrated bishops and writers of the Syriac Orthodox Church in the ninth century. A native of Balad in northern Mesopotamia, he became a monk and later served for many years as bishop in the region of Mosul. He wrote extensively. His works include biblical commentaries, a Hexaemeron, a treatise on Paradise, explanations of the liturgy and sacraments, homilies, and a treatise On the Soul. Later Syriac scholars, especially Dionysius bar Salibi, drew heavily on his work.

Moses of Khoren (Movses Khorenatsi) was an Armenian historian and the author of the History of the Armenians. It was the first attempt at a full history of Armenia, running from the nation's legendary origins to the fifth century. He presented himself as a young disciple of Mesrop Mashtots who wrote at the request of Prince Sahak Bagratuni. Since the nineteenth century, however, scholars have disputed his date, and some place him between the seventh and ninth centuries. Known as the "father of Armenian history," he preserves unique pre-Christian oral traditions. The Armenian Church honours him as one of the Holy Translators.

Narsai (c. 399 – c. 502) was a Syriac poet-theologian and one of the most important writers of the early Church of the East. He taught at the School of Edessa and later headed it. After leaving Edessa he became the leading teacher of the School of Nisibis. His theology follows the exegetical tradition of Theodore of Mopsuestia. Eighty-one of his mēmrē, or verse homilies, survive. He is ranked with Jacob of Serugh, second only to Ephrem the Syrian. Called the "Harp of the Holy Spirit," he is venerated as a saint in the churches descended from the Church of the East.

Naucratius of Stoudios (died 848) was a Byzantine monk, a disciple of Theodore the Studite and his successor as hegumen of the Stoudios monastery in Constantinople. He led the Studite community from Theodore's death in 826 until his own death in 848, a period that included the last phase of iconoclasm. He is chiefly known for his encyclical letter on Theodore's death. Addressed to the Studite monks, it describes their teacher's final days and death, and it is an important early witness to his life and veneration.

Nazarius was a Latin rhetorician and panegyrist of the early fourth century. Ausonius records that he taught rhetoric at Burdigala (Bordeaux). His one certainly authentic surviving work is a panegyric to Constantine the Great, delivered in 321. It marked the fifteenth anniversary of Constantine's accession and the fifth anniversary of his sons' elevation to the rank of Caesar. The speech is preserved among the XII Panegyrici Latini and praises Constantine's campaigns, especially his victory over Maxentius. An earlier panegyric of 313 has sometimes been attributed to him, but differences of style and vocabulary make this unlikely.

Nemesius of Emesa (fl. c. 390–400) was a Greek Christian philosopher. The title of his only known work names him bishop of Emesa, modern Homs in Syria. That work, On the Nature of Man (De natura hominis), tries to build a Christian account of human beings. It draws on Platonic, Aristotelian and Stoic philosophy and on the medicine of Galen. It discusses the soul, the body and its functions, free will and divine providence, and it is known for linking different mental faculties to the cavities of the brain. The treatise was widely read in later Byzantine, Arabic and medieval Latin thought.

Nestorius (c. 386–c. 451) was a theologian trained in the Antiochene tradition and Archbishop of Constantinople from 428 to 431. He hesitated over calling Mary Theotokos ("God-bearer") and preferred Christotokos ("Christ-bearer"), in order to keep Christ's divine and human natures distinct. This brought him into conflict with Cyril of Alexandria. The Council of Ephesus condemned and deposed him in 431, and he died in exile in Egypt. Most of his writings were destroyed, though some letters and sermons survive. His late apology, the Bazaar of Heracleides, is preserved in Syriac and has led scholars to reassess his Christology.

Nicephorus I (c. 758–828), also called the Confessor, was a Byzantine historian and theologian who served as Patriarch of Constantinople from 806 to 815. He had been an imperial secretary and was still a layman when he was chosen as patriarch. He defended the veneration of icons, and when Emperor Leo V revived iconoclasm he was deposed and exiled, dying in a monastery. His Short History (Breviarium) covers Byzantine events from 602 to 769, and he also wrote a brief universal chronicle. His theological works include the Antirrhetici against Constantine V, the Apologeticus and other defences of images.

Nicephorus the Chartophylax was a Byzantine cleric who held the office of chartophylax, the keeper of archives and records, at the Great Church of Constantinople. He is known only through his letters, which deal with questions of canon law and church discipline. His dates are uncertain. He is usually placed around the late eighth or early ninth century, but this dating is not secure. His surviving letters are of interest for the history of Byzantine penitential and canonical practice.

Nicephorus the Presbyter is the name given as author of the Greek Life of Andrew the Fool (Vita S. Andreae Sali), a long hagiographical work about a holy fool in Constantinople. In the text he presents himself as a priest of Hagia Sophia and as Andrew's friend and eyewitness, and he places the saint in the fifth century. Modern scholars treat this claim as a literary device and date the work to the tenth century. Nothing is known about him beyond the Life itself. The work is known for its vivid picture of city life and its apocalyptic passages.

Niketas David Paphlagon was a prolific Byzantine Greek writer of the late ninth and early tenth centuries. Older scholarship placed his death around 890, but more recent research suggests he lived well into the tenth century. A disciple of Arethas of Caesarea, he opposed the fourth marriage of Emperor Leo VI. For this he was imprisoned and then confined to seclusion. His many works include encomia and about fifty hagiographies. Among them is a Life of Patriarch Ignatios that also serves as a polemic against Photios. He also wrote a commentary on the Psalms, exegesis of Gregory of Nazianzus's poems and a treatise on the end times.

Nicetas of Byzantium (Nicetas Byzantius) was a Byzantine theologian and polemicist of the ninth century. He was active in Constantinople under the emperors Michael III and Basil I, in the circle of the patriarch Photios. He is known chiefly for apologetic writings against other faiths and confessions. His Refutation of the Qur'an is one of the earliest detailed Byzantine critiques of Islam, and it is based on a Greek translation of the Qur'anic text. He also wrote replies to letters from an Armenian ruler that defend Chalcedonian Christology. Writings against the Latin teaching on the procession of the Holy Spirit are also attributed to him.

Nicetas of Nicaea was a Byzantine Greek churchman and writer of the eleventh century, probably active between about 1050 and 1080. Little is known of his life. His writings belong to the debates between the Greek and Latin churches that followed the breach of 1054. Works attributed to him include a short treatise on the schism, which discusses the points disputed between Constantinople and Rome, and some letters. The synodal edict of 1054 against the papal legates is also connected with his name.

Nicetas of Remesiana (c. 335 – c. 414) was a Latin Christian bishop, theologian and saint. He was bishop of Remesiana in the Roman province of Dacia Mediterranea, near modern Bela Palanka in Serbia. His friend Paulinus of Nola praised his missionary work among the Bessi and other Balkan peoples. Nicetas wrote instructions for candidates preparing for baptism, including De ratione fidei, De Spiritus Sancti potentia and an explanation of the Creed, which is an early witness to the phrase "communion of saints." He also wrote on vigils and on psalmody. Some scholars attribute the Te Deum to him, but this remains uncertain.

Niketas Stethatos (Latin Nicetas Pectoratus, c. 1005 – c. 1090) was a Byzantine monk of the Stoudios monastery in Constantinople, a mystical theologian, and a saint of the Eastern Orthodox Church. He was a disciple of Symeon the New Theologian, whose writings he edited and spread, and he wrote the fullest biography of him, the Life of Symeon. His three centuries of chapters on the practical, natural and gnostic life appear in the Philokalia. Around 1054 he wrote polemical works against Latin practices, including the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist.

Nicetius (French: Nizier; died probably 566) was bishop of Trier from about 526. He was a monk from the Auvergne whom the Frankish king Theuderic I appointed to the see. He was the most important early bishop of Trier under Frankish rule. He restored churches in the region and boldly rebuked Frankish kings for their conduct, which led to a period of exile. Two of his letters survive. One warns Emperor Justinian against heresy. The other urges Queen Chlodosuinda to turn her Lombard husband Alboin away from Arianism. Gregory of Tours and Venantius Fortunatus both preserve accounts of his life.

Nicholas I Mystikos (852–925) was Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 901 to 907 and again from 912 until his death. Born in Italy, he was a friend of Patriarch Photius and served Emperor Leo VI as mystikos, an imperial secretary. He was deposed after opposing Leo's fourth marriage and was restored in 912. After his return he led the regency for the young Constantine VII and dealt with the threat from Simeon I of Bulgaria. His large collection of letters is a major source for Byzantine politics and church affairs. A homily on the capture of Thessalonica is also attributed to him.

Nilus of Ancyra (died c. 430) was a Greek ascetic writer and monastic leader near Ancyra in Galatia. He is said to have been a disciple and defender of John Chrysostom. Later tradition placed him on Mount Sinai and called him Nilus of Sinai, but modern scholars largely reject that account. He is known for a large collection of letters, often short, giving spiritual and scriptural counsel, and for treatises on monastic life, voluntary poverty and the vices. Several works handed down under his name, notably De oratione and the treatise on the eight evil thoughts, are now attributed to Evagrius Ponticus.

Nonnus of Panopolis was a Greek poet from Panopolis (modern Akhmim) in the Egyptian Thebaid. He probably lived in the fifth century AD and is regarded as the most important Greek epic poet of the Roman imperial period. He wrote the Dionysiaca, a 48-book epic in Homeric hexameters on the life of Dionysus and his expedition to India. He also wrote a hexameter paraphrase of the Gospel of John, known as the Metabole. Scholars still debate how his pagan mythological epic relates to his Christian poem and in what order he wrote them.

Notker Labeo (c. 950–1022), also called Notker III or Notker the German, was a Benedictine monk and teacher at the Abbey of Saint Gall. He is best known for his translations of Latin school texts into Old High German, often with commentary. These include Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, Martianus Capella and works of Aristotle's logic, as well as the Psalter with its canticles and catechetical texts. Medieval commentary on Aristotle effectively begins with him, and his work is a major witness to Old High German prose. Five short essays on music are also attributed to him. His epithet Labeo means "the thick-lipped".

Novatian (c. 200 – c. 258) was a Roman presbyter and theologian. He was the first major Roman theologian to write in Latin. In 251, during the dispute over readmitting Christians who had lapsed in the Decian persecution, he took a strict line against Pope Cornelius. Three bishops consecrated him as a rival bishop of Rome, and he was excommunicated. The Novatianist church that followed him lasted for centuries. His chief work is the treatise On the Trinity. He also wrote On the Jewish Meats, and On the Public Shows and On the Good of Chastity, which were handed down among Cyprian's writings.

Novatus Catholicus was an obscure Latin Christian writer, probably of the fifth or sixth century. Almost nothing is known of his life, and his exact date and place are uncertain. The epithet "Catholicus" may have been meant to set him apart from the Novatianist schismatics. He is known only as the author of a short moral treatise, De humilitate et obedientia et de calcanda superbia ("On humility and obedience and on trampling down pride"). It praises humility and obedience as the basis of the Christian and monastic life and warns against the dangers of pride.

Oecumenius, sometimes called the Rhetor, is the name attached to several Greek commentaries on the New Testament. These were not all written by the same person or in the same period. The most important is a Commentary on the Apocalypse, now dated to the late sixth or early seventh century and thought to come from Asia Minor. It is the earliest surviving Greek commentary on Revelation. Its author was once identified with a tenth-century bishop of Trikka in Thessaly, but that is now rejected. It is uncertain whether he was the Count Oecumenius to whom Severus of Antioch wrote. The catena commentaries on Acts and the Epistles that carry his name are pseudonymous.

Óengus mac Óengobann, known as Óengus the Culdee or Óengus of Tallaght, was an Irish monk, bishop and writer active in the first quarter of the ninth century. He was associated with the Céli Dé reform movement and with the monasteries of Clonenagh and Tallaght, where he worked under Máel Ruain. He is held to be the author of the Félire Óengusso, a metrical Irish calendar of saints for every day of the year, and possibly of the Martyrology of Tallaght. The annals place his death on 11 March 824, but some scholars argue for a later date. Little of his life is reliably attested.

Olympiodorus the Deacon was a Greek Christian biblical exegete who served as a deacon in Alexandria during the first half of the sixth century. He is not the same person as his contemporary, the Neoplatonist philosopher Olympiodorus the Younger. His surviving works include full commentaries on Ecclesiastes and Job. Many of his comments on Jeremiah, Lamentations and Baruch survive only as fragments in the catenae, the anthologies of patristic exegesis. His interpretation is mostly literal and moral, following the Alexandrian commentary tradition.

Optatus was bishop of Milevis (Mileve) in Roman Numidia, North Africa, in the later fourth century. He is known for his treatise against the Donatist bishop Parmenian of Carthage, usually called Against the Donatists. He wrote it around 366–367 and expanded it later, probably in the 380s, into seven books. Optatus traced the history of the Donatist schism and defended the unity of the Catholic Church, its communion with the see of Rome, and the view that sacraments are valid whoever the minister is. A collection of documents on the schism's origins comes down with the work. Augustine praised him, and he is venerated as a saint.

Orientius was a Latin Christian poet of fifth-century Gaul. He is usually identified with Saint Orientius, bishop of Auch in Aquitaine, who was active in the 430s and is said to have died around 439, though the identification is not certain. His main work is the Commonitorium, a didactic poem of about 1,036 lines in elegiac couplets, written around 430. It urges readers toward salvation and warns them against sin, particularly in the turmoil after the barbarian invasions of Gaul. Some shorter poems and prayers are also attributed to him, but several of these attributions are doubtful.

Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253/254), also called Adamantius, was an early Christian theologian, biblical scholar and ascetic. He taught first in Alexandria and later at Caesarea in Palestine, where he founded a Christian school. He wrote a huge amount, including the Hexapla, a multi-column edition of the Old Testament; On First Principles, an early systematic theology; the apologetic Against Celsus; and many commentaries and homilies that read Scripture allegorically. He was tortured in the Decian persecution and died a few years later. His bold speculations, later called Origenism, made him both deeply influential and controversial.

Paulus Orosius (c. 375/385 – c. 420) was a Latin priest, historian and theologian, probably from Bracara Augusta (Braga) in Gallaecia. He was a disciple of Augustine of Hippo, who sent him to Palestine in 415. There he opposed Pelagius at a synod in Jerusalem and was later entrusted with relics of Saint Stephen. His writings include a memorandum to Augustine on the errors of the Priscillianists and Origenists and a Liber apologeticus against Pelagianism. He is best known for the Seven Books of History against the Pagans, a Christian universal history that was widely read throughout the Middle Ages.

Horsiesi (Horsiesius, Orsisius; died c. 380) was an Egyptian monk and one of the early leaders of the Pachomian coenobitic communities in Upper Egypt. A disciple of Pachomius, he became head of the koinonia after Petronius died in 346. Amid internal dissent he handed effective leadership to Theodore, then took up the office again after Theodore's death in 368. His surviving writings include letters and instructions in Coptic. He is best known for the Liber Orsiesii, a spiritual testament for his monks that Jerome translated into Latin.

Hosius (Ossius) of Corduba (c. 256 – c. 357/359) was bishop of Córdoba in Roman Hispania. He was a leading defender of Nicene, homoousian Christianity during the Arian controversy. He was a close adviser to Constantine the Great and probably presided at the First Council of Nicaea (325). He also presided at the Council of Serdica (343), whose canons preserve his proposals. In his letter to Emperor Constantius II, he refused to condemn Athanasius. Near the end of his life, he was pressured into accepting the creed of Sirmium. He is venerated as a confessor.

Otfrid of Weissenburg (c. 800 – after 870) was a monk of the abbey of Weissenburg, now Wissembourg in Alsace. He wrote the Evangelienbuch, a gospel harmony in rhyming couplets in the South Rhine Franconian dialect of Old High German, thought to have been completed between 863 and 871. He sent the poem with a Latin dedicatory letter to Archbishop Liutbert of Mainz, in which he explains his reasons for writing in the vernacular. Otfrid is the earliest German poet known by name from his own work, and his poem is the first major use of end rhyme in German verse.

Otloh (Othloh, Othlo) of St Emmeram (c. 1010 – c. 1070) was a Benedictine monk, scribe, teacher and writer at the abbey of St Emmeram in Regensburg, and also a composer and music theorist. His Latin writings include saints' lives, among them a Life of Saint Boniface, a book of proverbs, a book of visions and a notably personal autobiographical account of his spiritual temptations and doubts. He is also known for a prayer he wrote in Latin and also produced in a German version. Known as Othlohs Gebet, it is an important early text in Old High German.

Latinius Pacatus Drepanius (fl. 389–393) was a Latin rhetorician and panegyrist from Gaul, probably Aquitaine, and a friend of the poet Ausonius. He is known for a panegyric delivered before Emperor Theodosius I in Rome in 389. The speech celebrates the emperor's victory over the usurper Magnus Maximus and is preserved in the collection known as the Panegyrici Latini. It is an important source for the history and court rhetoric of the late fourth century. Pacatus later held high office, serving as proconsul of Africa and as comes rerum privatarum.

Pachomius the Great (born c. 287–292, died 348) was an Egyptian monk generally regarded as the founder of Christian cenobitic, or communal, monasticism. Born to pagan parents in Upper Egypt, he became a Christian after serving as a conscript soldier and trained under the hermit Palaemon. Around 320 he founded a monastery at Tabennisi in the Thebaid, which grew into a federation of communities, the Koinonia. His Rule, written in Coptic and translated into Latin by Jerome, shaped later monastic legislation. His Instructions and letters also survive. He died during an epidemic in 348.

Pacian (Pacianus, c. 310–391) was bishop of Barcelona in Roman Hispania and one of the earliest Latin Christian writers from Spain. Jerome praised him for his eloquence and his chaste life. His surviving works include three letters to Sympronian, a Novatianist who denied that the Church could forgive grave sins. In the first letter he writes the famous line "Christianus mihi nomen est, catholicus vero cognomen" ("Christian is my name, Catholic my surname"). He also wrote an exhortation to penance (Paraenesis) and a sermon on baptism. Together these are important evidence for early penitential discipline.

Palladius of Helenopolis (c. 363 – c. 420s), also called Palladius of Galatia, was a Greek Christian monk, chronicler and bishop of Helenopolis in Bithynia. He was a disciple of Evagrius Ponticus and lived for years among the monks of Egypt. He was also a devoted supporter of John Chrysostom. His best-known work, the Lausiac History, is a collection of portraits of desert ascetics dedicated to the court official Lausus. It became a key source for early monasticism. He also wrote the Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom. He is venerated as a saint in the Coptic and Syriac Orthodox churches.

Pamphilus of Caesarea (late 3rd century – c. 309/310) was a priest of Caesarea Maritima in Palestine and the leading biblical scholar of his generation. He studied at Alexandria, then expanded the library at Caesarea that Origen had begun, copying and correcting manuscripts of the Scriptures, including Origen's Hexapla. He taught Eusebius of Caesarea, who took the name "Pamphili" and wrote a Life of him that is now lost. While imprisoned during the persecution under Maximinus Daia, Pamphilus wrote an Apology for Origen with Eusebius. Only its first book survives, in Rufinus's Latin translation. He was martyred in about 309 or 310.

Pantaenus (died c. 200) was a Christian teacher, probably of Sicilian origin, who led the Catechetical School of Alexandria from about 180. He was the school's earliest well-attested head, although some accounts make Athenagoras his predecessor. Eusebius says he had been a Stoic philosopher before becoming a Christian, and that he travelled as a missionary to "India", where he found a Gospel of Matthew in Hebrew said to have been left there by the apostle Bartholomew. He taught Clement of Alexandria. None of his own writings survive, and he is known only through a few fragments and reports in other writers.

Papias was a Greek Christian writer and bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia, in Asia Minor. He was active in the early second century and is counted among the Apostolic Fathers. He gathered oral traditions about Jesus and the apostles from people such as John the Elder and the daughters of Philip, and wrote them down in five books titled Exposition of the Sayings of the Lord, usually dated to around 110. The work is lost. Only fragments survive, quoted mainly by Irenaeus and Eusebius. These include his much-debated statements about the origins of the Gospels of Mark and Matthew, and his millenarian teaching.

Paschasius the Deacon (died c. 512) was a deacon of the Roman church, admired for his learning and charity. He wrote De Spiritu Sancto, a treatise in two books defending the full divinity of the Holy Spirit. Eugippius sent him his memoir of Severinus of Noricum so that Paschasius could write a formal Life. In a surviving letter, Paschasius declined and judged the memoir sufficient as it was. In the Laurentian schism he sided with Laurentius against Pope Symmachus. Gregory the Great's Dialogues tell how he was seen after death, still atoning in the baths at Angulus.

Paterius (died 606) was a Latin churchman who served as a notary to Pope Gregory I (590–604) and later became bishop of Brescia. He is known as a compiler of Gregory's writings. His only surviving work, known as the Liber testimoniorum or Liber de expositione Veteris ac Novi Testamenti, is an anthology of Gregory's biblical exegesis. It gathers passages from Gregory's various works and arranges them in the order of the biblical texts they explain. The collection was widely copied in the Middle Ages and survives in more than 120 complete or partial manuscripts.

Patrick (Patricius) was a fifth-century Romano-British Christian missionary and bishop in Ireland. His exact dates are uncertain. As a youth he was captured by Irish raiders and held as a slave. He later escaped, then returned to Ireland to preach. Two Latin writings are generally accepted as his: the Confessio, an account of his life and calling, and the Letter to Coroticus, which condemns a British chieftain whose soldiers killed or enslaved newly baptised converts. Canons and synodal decrees bearing his name are of disputed or later origin. He is venerated as the patron saint of Ireland.

Paul was a Latin monastic abbot of the sixth century. Together with an abbot named Stephen, he is named as co-author of the Regula Pauli et Stephani, a short rule addressed to monks (Regula ad monachos). It sets out practical regulations for community life, prayer and discipline. Almost nothing is known about his life. Scholars disagree on where the rule was written, with both Italy and Spain proposed, and its date can only be placed approximately in the sixth century.

Paul of Chalcis was a Greek-speaking presbyter and archimandrite, the head of a monastic community, in fourth-century Syria. He is known only as co-author, with Acacius, of a letter to Epiphanius of Salamis, written around 374–377. The letter asked Epiphanius to write a full account of the heresies. Epiphanius answered with a letter of reply, and both letters stand at the head of his Panarion, the treatise against eighty heresies that their request prompted. Beyond this exchange, nothing certain is known of his life.

Paul of Emesa (Latin Paulus Emesenus) was bishop of Emesa, modern Homs in Syria, during the Nestorian controversy that followed the Council of Ephesus in 431. In 432–433 John of Antioch sent him to Alexandria as his envoy to Cyril. His negotiations helped produce the Formula of Reunion of 433, which reconciled the Antiochene and Alexandrian churches. Paul preached homilies in Alexandria with Cyril present, in which he affirmed that Mary is Theotokos. These homilies survive with letters and short documents among the acts of the Ephesine controversy.

Paul of Mérida (Paulus Emeritensis) is the deacon of Mérida in Visigothic Spain traditionally named as the author of the Lives of the Fathers of Mérida (Vitas Sanctorum Patrum Emeretensium), written around the 630s or 640s. Many scholars now treat the work as anonymous, so the attribution is uncertain. The work tells of miracles linked to the shrine of Saint Eulalia and of sixth-century bishops of Mérida, including Paul, Fidelis and Masona. Masona's conflict with the Arian king Leovigild is a central theme. It is an important source for Visigothic Hispania.

Paul the Deacon (Paulus Diaconus, c. 720s–796/799) was a Lombard Benedictine monk, scholar and historian. Born to a noble family in Friuli, he was educated at the Lombard court at Pavia. He later became a monk at Monte Cassino and spent several years at Charlemagne's court. His chief work is the unfinished History of the Lombards, which runs to 744. He also wrote a Roman History, a history of the bishops of Metz, a Life of Gregory the Great, poems and letters. He compiled a homiliary for Charlemagne, and the hymn Ut queant laxis is traditionally attributed to him.

Paul the Persian (Paulus Persa) was a sixth-century Christian theologian and philosopher. Greek texts preserve his debate with the Manichaean Photinus, held in Constantinople around 527. In it Paul defends Christian teaching against Manichaean dualism, and the records include Photinus's statements and Paul's replies. Paul the Persian is also known for a commentary in Syriac on Aristotle's logic, written for the Sasanian king Khosrow I (r. 531–579), which later influenced Islamic philosophy. It is uncertain whether the debater and the philosopher were the same person. Some scholars identify him with Paul of Nisibis or Paul of Basra.

Paul the Silentiary (Paulus Silentiarius, died c. 575–580) was a Greek poet at the court of Justinian I in Constantinople, where he held the office of silentiarius, a palace official charged with keeping order. He is best known for his hexameter ekphrasis of Hagia Sophia, recited in 562–563 at the rededication of the church after its dome had been rebuilt, and for a companion description of its ambo. He also wrote a poem on the Pythian hot springs in Bithynia and many epigrams, among them love poems, preserved in the Greek Anthology.

Paulinus II of Aquileia (c. 726 – 802 or 804) was a priest, theologian and poet, and one of the leading scholars of the Carolingian Renaissance. He served as Patriarch of Aquileia in northeastern Italy from 787 until his death. He took part in synods that condemned Spanish Adoptionism and wrote against it. He also supported church reform and the addition of the Filioque to the Nicene Creed. He arranged the peaceful Christianisation of the Avars and Alpine Slavs, so he is called the apostle of the Slovenes. His Liber exhortationis is a book of moral guidance written for a layman, Duke Eric of Friuli.

Paulinus was a Latin Christian poet active in southern Gaul in the early fifth century. He is known only as the author of the Epigramma Paulini, a short verse dialogue written soon after the barbarian invasions of Gaul that began in 406. In it, the speakers attribute the disasters of the age to moral laxity among Christians and call for repentance. He is sometimes identified with Paulinus, bishop of Béziers around 419, but this identification is uncertain, and nothing else about his life is securely known.

Paulinus of Milan, also called Paulinus the Deacon, was a Latin cleric of the early fifth century who served as notary to Ambrose of Milan and later became a deacon in North Africa. At Carthage in 411 he accused Caelestius, a follower of Pelagius, of heresy. He later wrote the Libellus adversus Caelestium to Pope Zosimus as part of the same dispute. At Augustine's request he wrote the Life of Ambrose, usually dated to about 422. It is the only life of Ambrose based on contemporary knowledge. A short treatise on the blessings of the patriarchs is also attributed to him.

Paulinus of Nola (c. 354–431), born Pontius Meropius Paulinus, was a Latin Christian poet, letter-writer and bishop. A wealthy aristocrat from Bordeaux and a pupil of Ausonius, he held the posts of suffect consul and governor of Campania. Encouraged by his wife Therasia, he was baptized, gave up his wealth for an ascetic life and settled at Nola near the shrine of Saint Felix. He later became bishop there. His Carmina include yearly poems for Felix's feast. His Epistulae include letters to Augustine, Jerome, Sulpicius Severus and other leading Christians. Contemporaries held him up as a model of renunciation.

Paulinus of Pella (377 – after 461) was a Latin Christian poet. He was born at Pella in Macedonia, was the grandson of the poet Ausonius, and grew up in Bordeaux in Gaul. He is known for the Eucharisticos ("Thanksgiving"), an autobiographical poem in hexameters that he wrote in old age, around 459. In it he thanks God for the course of his life. He recalls a privileged youth, losing his estates during the Gothic invasions, serving under the usurper Priscus Attalus, and later years of poverty. The poem is an important witness to life in fifth-century Gaul as Roman rule in the West declined.

Paulinus of Périgueux was a Latin Christian poet of later fifth-century Gaul, active around 460–475. Little is known of his life. His main work is De vita sancti Martini, a hexameter epic in six books on Martin of Tours. It reworks the prose writings of Sulpicius Severus and a record of later miracles provided by Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, who encouraged the project. Shorter poems also survive. De visitatione nepotuli sui tells how his grandson was healed through Martin's intercession, and De orantibus is linked with Martin's basilica at Tours. Medieval tradition sometimes confused him with Paulinus of Nola.

Pelagius (c. 354–c. 418) was an ascetic Christian teacher, probably of British origin, who taught in Rome around 400 and later went to North Africa and Palestine. He stressed human free will and moral responsibility, and he denied that Adam's sin was passed on to his descendants. Augustine of Hippo strongly opposed these views. A synod at Diospolis acquitted Pelagius in 415, but his teaching was condemned at Carthage in 418. His surviving works include a commentary on the Pauline epistles, long passed down under Jerome's name, and the Letter to Demetrias.
